client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Gerald, good to meet you — well, sort of meet you, through a screen. Gotta love modern medicine, right? [small laugh] So Dr. Patterson sent over a referral, said you two had a chat at your last checkup. I'd love to just start by hearing from you — what was that conversation like, from your end?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... it was fine, I guess. She's a good doctor — been seeing her, oh, fifteen years now. She mentioned my liver numbers were a little off and said maybe I should talk to somebody. I wasn't... I don't know. Wasn't really expecting that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it caught you a little off guard. You went in for a regular visit and came out with homework — and I'm apparently the homework. [light tone] What did you make of what she said, about the liver?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't think it's as serious as maybe she made it sound. I'm not — I'm not somebody who's drinking all day or anything like that. I just have a few drinks in the evening, it helps me wind down. I've always done that, sort of. Maybe a bit more since I retired, but... I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Since you retired — tell me more about that. What's retirement actually been like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's... hm. [long pause] People don't tell you how quiet it gets. I worked thirty-two years at the same company. Every day there's somewhere to be, people who — they need you, in a way. Then one day it's just... nothing. My wife passed three years ago. Kids are in different states. I call on Sundays but it's not the same. The evenings are the hardest. I started having a drink after dinner and it just... became two, then three. Gives me something to do, I suppose. That sounds pathetic when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound pathetic. Not even a little. It sounds like you lost a lot at once — your wife, the structure of work, the sense that somebody needed you to show up. And the drinking moved in to fill some of those gaps. And for a while... maybe it did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet] Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I never thought about it that way but that's — yeah. I mean, it doesn't actually help, I know that. I wake up feeling worse and I'm still alone. Nothing's changed. I've been thinking about it more since she brought up my liver. I've watched people go down that road. I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you don't want that — and I'm hearing something underneath it too, something about more than just avoiding being sick. If things were actually good, not just okay — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hm. [pause] I guess I'd like to have somewhere to be again. Something to look forward to. I used to volunteer at the library — there was a program, helping kids learn to read. Stopped going when Margaret got sick and just never went back. Maybe I could do that again. And I'd like to just... feel okay when I wake up. I think I've kind of forgotten what that feels like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I take a moment to pull together what you've shared today? You came in because your doctor was worried — and honestly, part of you was too, even if you weren't quite ready to say it at first. You told me about retiring, about losing Margaret, about how the evenings got quiet and the drinking crept in to fill that space. And you've been clear-eyed about the fact that it's not actually working — you wake up worse, not better, and you're still alone. But when I asked what good could look like, you didn't hesitate long before you mentioned the library, those kids, feeling okay in the morning. That's not nothing, Gerald. That's a lot to work with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, it's — yeah. I think I needed to say some of that out loud to somebody. Been sitting with it for a while on my own. I'm not saying I've got it all figured out, but... I think I want to try. I really do. It's worth trying.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you came in today. I know walk-in visits can feel a little... uncertain. You don't always know what you're walking into. So I just want to start by asking — what brought you through the door?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor called me. About some bloodwork. She said some numbers were off and that I should — I don't know, she said I should talk to someone. I'm not really sure what I'm supposed to be doing here, honestly. I've never done... this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So she saw something in those results that concerned her enough to pick up the phone and call you directly. And that call landed you here, even though you weren't sure what to expect.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I know what she thinks is going on. I've been drinking more than I used to. But it's — look, I've had a really hard year. A really, really hard year. I just needed something to take the edge off at night. It's not like I'm... I don't know, I'm not some kind of alcoholic or whatever. I just... I've been struggling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to justify yourself to me. I'm not here to put a label on anything. I'm just... I'm curious about this hard year you're describing. What's been happening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My husband passed. Eight months ago. Harold. And everyone said oh, time heals, you'll be okay, and then they just... stopped calling. My kids have their own lives, I get it. But I come home to that house every single day and it is just... quiet. And a glass of wine helps me sleep. That's all it is. I'm not — I can stop whenever I want, it just... it helps me get through the night. I don't see why that's such a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You lost Harold... and then in a way, you lost everyone else too. People said the right things and then drifted away. And you've been carrying all of that — alone — in a house that used to have someone in it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — God. I don't even sleep in the bedroom anymore. I sleep on the couch because the bedroom still smells like him and I just... I can't go in there. I can't. And the wine, it just makes the quiet less loud. You know? It makes it so I can actually breathe for a few hours without feeling like I'm going to fall apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been surviving something enormous. Grief like that — it doesn't just live in your head, it lives in the bedroom, in the quiet, in every corner of that house. And the fact that you're sitting here right now, even when you weren't sure why you came... that took something real. I want you to know that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel like it took anything. I feel like I'm disappearing. Like I'm just... fading. Harold was the strong one. He always knew what to do and I just — I look at those lab results and I think, what am I doing? Am I actually trying to hurt myself? I don't think I am. But I don't know. I really don't know anymore. He would be so disappointed in me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard today, because I think you've said some really important things. You lost Harold eight months ago, and with him you lost your footing — in the house, in your relationships, in yourself. The drinking became a way to survive the nights. And now your body is sending up a signal, and part of you — the part that's sitting here — is wondering if this is actually working anymore. And underneath all of that, I hear someone who still cares deeply. About Harold. About what he'd think. About herself. So I'm wondering... is there one small thing — doesn't have to be big — that feels even a little bit possible from here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... maybe I could call my daughter. I keep not calling because I don't want to be a burden but Harold always used to say she worries because she loves us. So maybe I should just... let her worry a little. And maybe — coming back here. Talking like this. I think I could do that. I think I want to do that.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, before we get into anything formal — I just want to hear from you. In your own words, what's been going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... my doctor's been on me about my liver, and then the thing at the hardware store. I work there part-time, just... just to get out of the house, really. Showed up one morning and I wasn't, uh... I wasn't in good shape. They said I had to come here or they'd let me go. [pause] Since I retired — three years now — and then my wife passed, about two years back... the days are just long. Real long. I drink more than I used to. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The days got long after she died, and drinking filled some of that space.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] Look, I've been to counselors before. Two of them. Nothing stuck. And I'm not saying that to be difficult, I just... I'm 65. My liver's already bad. My wife's gone. My kids have their own lives, they don't call much. I don't really see how sitting in a chair talking about my feelings changes any of that. I'm not trying to be rude. I just don't see it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've tried this twice before, it didn't work, and you're back again anyway. I want to say something about that — that's not nothing. Most people in your position stop showing up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I didn't have much of a choice this time. [sighs] But yeah, I'm here. I don't want to lose the store job. It's the only reason I get out of bed on Tuesdays and Thursdays. [quieter] I just don't know if I can actually do it. Stop, or even just... cut back. I've told myself that before and it lasts maybe a week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So those Tuesday and Thursday mornings — that job — that's one of the last things anchoring you to something. And you're scared of losing it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's right, actually. [pause] And I guess when I really sit with it... I don't want to be the guy who just drinks himself to death alone in his house. I coached Little League for fifteen years. Fifteen years. My grandkids — I haven't seen them since October because my son thinks I'm a mess. And he's not wrong. [pause] I don't know. Maybe I do want something different. I think part of me does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would different actually look like for you — not for your son, not for the store — for you specifically?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want to see my grandkids again. That's the big one. And just... wake up not feeling like garbage. Feel like I'm still worth something, you know? Like I still have a reason to be here. [pause] I don't know how to get there. But I think — and I mean this differently than when I've said it before — I think I actually want to try. Not just go through the motions so somebody stops bothering me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what you've told me today, because I think it matters. You walked in here not believing this would work — you said that flat out. And in the same conversation, you told me there's a part-time job that gets you out of bed twice a week, grandkids you want back in your life, fifteen years of showing up for kids on a Little League field, and a man inside you who doesn't want to disappear quietly. You said you want to feel worth something. That's not a man who's finished. That's a man who still has things worth fighting for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. [long pause] Nobody's ever said it back to me like that before. [clears throat] Yeah. Yeah, I think... I think I'm ready to do this. Not because I got sent here. Because I'm tired of the other way.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. It takes something to walk through that door. So... tell me a little about what brought you here — in your own words, whatever feels right to share.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm not sure I should even be here. I saw something on the VA website and I just... I don't know, I clicked on it. My daughter keeps saying I drink too much but she doesn't — I mean, it's not like I'm an alcoholic or anything. I hold it together. I go to the grocery store, I pay my bills. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is wondering if this is even the right place for you... and at the same time, something made you click on that link. Something brought you here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. It's just wine. I have a glass or two at night to wind down. Sometimes more. Since my husband passed — eight months ago — I just, the nights are really long and quiet and I can't sleep otherwise. It's not hurting anyone. It's not like I'm driving drunk or whatever. It helps.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You lost your husband eight months ago. And those nights... they're long. And silent. And the wine gives you some relief from that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's the only time it's quiet inside my head, you know? During the day I can keep busy, sort of. But at night it's just... everything comes in. All of it. And I don't — I haven't really talked to anyone. His friends stopped calling. My sister tried for a while but I kept telling her I was fine and eventually she... stopped. I pushed everyone away, I think. It's easier.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying this alone for eight months. Grieving alone. And I want you to know — that you're here, that you reached out even when you've been pulling away from everyone else... that tells me something about you. There's a part of you that hasn't given up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I know it's gotten worse. The drinking. I know that. I finish a bottle and I'll open another one and think, Earl would hate this. He really would. He'd be so worried about me right now. And I just — I don't know how to feel all of it without it swallowing me whole. It's so much. It's just so much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've shared a lot with me today, and I want to reflect some of it back. You came in not sure you belonged here. And in the space of this conversation, you've told me that the nights are unbearable, that you've pulled away from everyone who loves you, and that you know — in your own heart — that things have gotten harder. And you mentioned Earl. That he wouldn't want this for you. It sounds like he's still very much a part of how you see yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He is. He really is. I keep thinking — what would he say? He'd probably make some dumb joke to lighten the mood and then hug me for a long time. That's what he did. I miss that so much. And... yeah. I'm scared of what it feels like if I stop numbing it. But I think I'm also scared of what I'm turning into. I don't recognize myself lately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to say. What would it look like, do you think — even just a small step — toward not carrying all of this alone anymore?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... coming back here. Talking. I haven't actually talked about Earl — like really talked about him — to anyone. Not since the funeral. Maybe that's where I start. I think that's where I start.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... you're here. I'm guessing this wasn't exactly on your to-do list for today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It wasn't. I'm only here because a judge told me I had to be — let's be real clear about that. So whatever you're trying to get me to admit or confess or whatever, I'm not doing it. This whole thing is a joke. I had two drinks. Two. And I'm being treated like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I'm a menace or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two drinks, and somehow you ended up here. That's got to feel deeply unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It IS unfair. I'm not — okay, fine, I wasn't stone cold sober. A point-oh-nine. That's barely over the limit. But now I lose my license, I gotta do all this... my wife's already looking at me like — [stops] Look, what happens to my job if this gets out? I'm in sales. I drive. That's literally what I do. Nobody's thinking about that part.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your job, your license, your wife — there's a lot on the line right now. What else feels like it's at risk for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My kids. I've got a twelve-year-old girl and a nine-year-old boy and... after the first one, my daughter — she just looked at me different, you know? Like something shifted. She stopped asking me to come to her games for a while. [quietly] I never wanted to be that dad. My old man was — let's just say I know what that looks like from the other side. And I swore I'd never... [trails off, jaw tight]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to go there if you're not ready. But I want to name something — you just said you swore you'd never be that dad. That's not a small thing. That tells me a lot about what kind of man you're trying to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Knowing and doing are two different things, aren't they. [exhales slowly] I've told myself I'd cut back a hundred times. And I do — for a while. Then work gets crazy, or me and my wife get into it, and it's just... it's easy, you know? Everything else is hard and drinking is the one thing that's — I don't know. It works. For a few hours at least.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it gives you real relief when things pile up — and that part makes complete sense. And at the same time there's your daughter's face after the first DUI. Both those things are true at once. What's it like sitting with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's... it's awful. [pause] I'm not dumb. I can see what's happening. It's like I keep telling myself it's fine and then something like this blows up and I'm sitting here and... I don't know. Maybe there's actually something I need to deal with. I've just never — I don't talk about stuff. Never have. This is really weird for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in here furious today — and honestly, that made sense given everything. But underneath that, there's a guy who's scared about losing his livelihood, who still carries what he saw in his own father, who looks at his daughter and wants to be different. And just now, you said maybe there's something to actually deal with. That's not nothing — that's the first honest thing most people say in weeks of sessions.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] Yeah, I guess... I don't even know what that looks like. Actually dealing with it. But I — I can't keep doing this to them. To her. So... I don't know. Maybe I'm willing to figure that out. A little.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, you're back. I'll be honest — I wasn't a hundred percent sure you would be, not because I doubted you, just... last time felt pretty rough. So genuinely, I'm glad you came in. How's everything been since we talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I came back because my doctor basically made me feel like I was dying. My liver numbers or whatever. So yeah. But I don't actually think I have a problem — the labs just freaked me out a little. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you came in because the numbers scared you, even if another part isn't totally convinced there's really a problem.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not — look. I moved here a year ago. Alone. I don't know anyone. My family is twelve time zones away and half the time they're asleep when I'm awake. I drink because there is literally nothing else to do at 10pm in a studio apartment in a city where I know nobody. That's not a problem, that's just... that's just my life right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That 10pm part — what does that actually feel like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What does it feel like? It feels like silence. Like... a lot of silence. And I went to university here, I'm not stupid, I worked really hard to get to this country, and now I'm just... sitting alone drinking wine because I don't know how to make friends as a 29-year-old adult? It's embarrassing. I hate it. And I hate that I'm saying it to you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to be carrying — the embarrassment, the silence, being far from everyone you love, working that hard to get somewhere that turned out to be lonelier than you expected.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I guess. I just — I didn't think it would be this hard. I'm usually good at figuring things out. I haven't figured this out, and it's been a year, and the wine just... it takes the edge off. I'm not like — I'm not some alcoholic. I just haven't figured the other stuff out yet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If the wine wasn't doing that job — taking the edge off that 10pm silence — what would be? What would actually help?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Connection, I guess. Like actual human contact. Even just... one person I could call. I've thought about joining some kind of group or whatever, like a running club or something, I don't know. I keep talking myself out of it. Like it'll be awkward, I won't fit in, what's the point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You named it yourself — connection. And here's what I notice: you're sitting in this room right now, talking about something really uncomfortable, when part of you didn't even want to come back. That is you trying to figure it out. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I never thought of it like that. I guess I am... sort of trying. I just don't want to be doing this forever — the drinking, the sitting alone. I'm only 29. That's not... that's not supposed to be my life.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in today. That takes something, especially after the week you've just had. I don't have an agenda here — I'm not here to tell you what to do or what to think. I'm just genuinely curious what it's been like for you, coming out the other side of detox.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm only here because Marcus basically dragged me. I mean — I did the detox. Fine. It's done. But I want to be clear about something: my work hasn't suffered. Not once. My Q1 numbers were the strongest we've had in six years. Six years. So I'm not entirely sure what we're supposed to be talking about here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six years. That's not nothing — you've clearly built something you're proud of. And at the same time... you're sitting here. Even while part of you is questioning whether you need to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Marcus doesn't see it that way. Neither does... neither does Claire. My wife. She had this whole — she brought this list. Things I supposedly said, things I did. And I don't remember half of them, which I know how that sounds, I know exactly how that sounds, but... I don't know. I just. I don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you think about that list — the things Claire wrote down that you don't remember — what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... look, I'm not an idiot. Medically, I understand that a bottle a night is — I know that's not nothing. I know that. But the idea that she was scared of me? That I made her feel unsafe in our house? I don't recognize that person. I genuinely don't recognize him. And that's — that's what scares me a little, if I'm being honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That gap — between who you know yourself to be and what someone you love experienced — that's a genuinely hard thing to sit with. And you just named it out loud. That took honesty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My dad drank. Badly. I mean, we're talking — it was not a good house to grow up in. And I swore to myself, I swore, that I was different. That I'd built something different. And I have. I've provided for everyone, I've never missed a school thing, I've — but... maybe I've been telling myself that story for so long I stopped actually checking if it was still true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm following you, because there's a lot here. You came in today not fully convinced you needed to be. You've worked incredibly hard to build a life that looks nothing like the one you came from — and that matters. And underneath all of that, there's this quieter question starting to surface: whether the story you've been telling yourself about being different... might need a closer look. That's a heavy thing to carry into a room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. I think — I think I've been exhausted for a very long time. And I never let myself actually know that. The scotch just... it turned the volume down at the end of the day. Everything got quieter. I didn't think of it as a problem. I thought of it as the thing I'd earned. The reward for getting through another day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — not for Claire, not for Marcus — but just for you, to start figuring out what the end of the day could feel like without needing to turn the volume down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I haven't let myself think about that. Not really. But sitting here — I think maybe I want to find out. I'm 45. I've got time. I think I do. I'd like to believe that I do.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in today. I know walking into a new place, meeting someone new — that's not always easy. There's no agenda here, nothing you have to prove. I just want to get a sense of you and what's been going on. So... what brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. So my therapist, Dr. Reyes — she's the one who referred me. She said she thought someone who specializes in like... substance stuff... might be more useful than she could be. Which, I don't know, I wasn't totally sure how to take that. I guess it's about drinking. But I want to be upfront — I don't really think I have a problem problem. I just drink at social events. That's kind of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So Dr. Reyes sent you here, and you showed up — even with some uncertainty about whether it fits. I appreciate that. When you say you drink at social events... I'm curious what that actually looks like for you, in a typical situation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So... okay. Like, I have really bad anxiety. Like, diagnosed, been on meds, the whole thing. And social situations are just — they're a lot. So every time there's something — a work happy hour, a birthday, whatever — I need to have at least one drink before I can even walk in. Sometimes I'll have a glass of wine in my car in the parking lot before I go inside. Which I know is... I know. But without it I just freeze. I literally can't speak.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The alcohol is doing something really specific for you. It's the thing that unlocks the door — lets you actually get in the room and be there with people, when otherwise the anxiety would just slam it shut.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly that. And I hate it. I hate that I can't just be normal. Like everyone else at these things seems totally fine and I'm in the parking lot having a minor breakdown. And then I have two drinks and suddenly I'm laughing and talking and people seem to like me and I feel okay. But then I go home and I'm like... who was that? That wasn't really me. She borrowed my face for the night. I don't know, it's hard to explain.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes a lot of self-awareness — to notice that gap. Between the version of you that shows up with alcohol and whoever you feel like you actually are underneath that. That's not a small thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about it more lately. I'm 26 and I don't think I've been to a single social thing sober since like... sophomore year of college. Not one. And I've done therapy before — CBT, exposure stuff — and it helps a little but then I'm still in the parking lot with a travel bottle of wine, so. I don't know. Maybe nothing works for me. Or maybe I just haven't been honest enough about how much this runs my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to stay with that last thing you said — that it runs your life. When you let yourself imagine what it might feel like to be in one of those rooms and actually feel okay without the alcohol there... what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never really let myself go there because it just feels... impossible. But actually — okay, there was this one night a few weeks ago. My friend Maya's birthday. I had one drink instead of my usual like four, and at some point I was laughing at something she said and I had this weird moment where I thought, wait. Was that real? Was that actually me laughing? And it was. It was. And I wanted to cry a little because I was like, oh, she's in there. I'm in there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and stop me if anything feels off. You came today because someone you trust thought it might help — and some part of you agreed, even if you weren't sure why. Drinking has been your way of getting through something that genuinely feels unbearable without it. But lately there's this quiet voice asking whether it's actually helping, or just... standing in. And then Maya's birthday — that moment of laughing and realizing it was really you. That glimpse meant something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's it. I didn't expect you to get it that quickly, honestly. My last therapist took three sessions before she even asked why I drank. Um... I think I do want to figure this out. I'm scared. Like genuinely scared. But I think I'm ready to at least try.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to see you today. I know... coming in after everything that happened this week couldn't have been easy. How are you feeling right now, just being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't really know why I keep having to come back here. Like, I already said everything I was gonna say. And it's not like the ER thing was even that big a deal, everyone was freaking out over nothing. My mom literally called the school about it which is so... ugh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. It sounds like it feels like a lot of people around you are making this into something much bigger than you think it actually is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Because it IS. Like... every single person at that party was drinking. Every single one. I just happened to be the one who got sick, which — okay, fine, whatever, but that doesn't make me like, an alcoholic or whatever they're all acting like. I'm eighteen. This is what people do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And that feels deeply unfair — being singled out, being the one everyone's watching, when it felt like you weren't doing anything different from everyone else around you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It IS unfair. Like, I'm so tired of — no one's sending my friends here. No one's calling their moms. And now I have to sit here every week and talk about my feelings or whatever and it's just... I don't even — ugh. No offense but I hate this. I hate that they made me come here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No offense taken at all — I really mean that. And honestly? Saying that out loud, being real with me about how much you don't want to be here... that actually takes something. You still showed up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I didn't really have a choice. But um... I don't know. I was actually kind of scared in the hospital. Like, genuinely scared. I didn't think it was gonna get that bad. I thought I was just gonna sleep it off and wake up at home but then I woke up there and there were these tubes and my mom was crying and I just...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something really shifted in that moment for you. What was going through your mind when you were lying there and realized how scared you actually were?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just kept thinking like... what if it was worse? What if I hadn't woken up? And I know that probably sounds so dramatic but it was like — I don't actually want anything bad to happen to me. I just want to be normal. I want people to like me and not feel like I'm doing everything wrong all the time. I don't know. I don't want to end up there again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So underneath all of this — the drinking, the pressure, feeling like you have to keep up with everyone else — there's someone who really does want to be okay. Who got scared enough to start asking herself whether there might be another way to belong, to feel connected, without it having to go that far.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, I think so. I don't totally know how to do that yet but... maybe that's actually what I want to figure out. Like maybe that's why I keep coming back even when I say I don't want to.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... last week sounded rough from what you mentioned when you called. I want to hear it from you — what happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, it was — look, I slipped up. More than once. But it was parent-teacher conferences, and I had this one situation with a kid's family that just... it spiraled. I'm not making excuses, I just — the circumstances were not normal. It wasn't like a regular week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The week just kept coming at you — and by the time you got home, drinking was the only thing that felt like it gave you any breathing room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Sort of. I don't know if I'd put it exactly like that, but. Yeah. When everything piles up it's like — there's this pull. And I know what you're probably thinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think I'm thinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I need other coping strategies or whatever. That I'm using it as a crutch. And maybe — okay, fine, maybe I am. But right now it's the thing that actually works. I get home, I pour a drink, and my shoulders just... I can breathe again. You don't teach thirty eighth-graders all day and then go home and just, like, meditate. That's not real life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That relief is real. You're not imagining it. And it sounds like for a long time, it's been one of the only things that's reliably been there for you at the end of a hard day. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah but... I woke up Tuesday, I think it was Tuesday, and I just felt — god. I felt disgusting. And I had to go in. And I kept looking at my kids during first period and thinking, what if they can tell? What if a parent says something to the principal? I've been teaching for eleven years. I actually — I care about it. I don't want to be that guy. The one people feel sorry for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image of yourself — being the teacher people feel sorry for — that's clearly not who you are or who you want to be. You said you've been doing this eleven years and you care. What does the version of you who's not dragging himself through mornings look like? Like concretely — what's different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I used to run. Actually run, not just like walk around the block. I did a half marathon — this was six years ago maybe. And I slept better, I wasn't white-knuckling my coffee every morning. I don't know if I can get back there. That feels like a different person almost. But I think about it. What it felt like to wake up and just... not feel like garbage.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You had a really hard week — harder than most — and you slipped, and part of you wants to chalk it up to circumstances. But another part of you woke up Tuesday morning and couldn't shake what you saw in the mirror. You've got eleven years of work you're proud of, students you genuinely show up for, and somewhere in the back of your mind there's still this guy who ran a half marathon — who knows what it feels like to be on the other side of this. That guy hasn't gone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, I think that's — I mean, when you put it like that. I don't know. Maybe I'm not as far gone as I tell myself I am on the bad nights. I'm not ready to like, make some big announcement or whatever. But maybe I can just — start somewhere small. Something I can actually do.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Last time we left things pretty heavy. How's this week been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I don't even know where to start. My advisor sent me this email on Tuesday and it basically said my chapter draft was... 'not up to the standard expected at this stage.' Which I knew. I knew it wasn't good. But seeing it in writing is like — it's different. And then I just kind of shut down for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Knowing something and having it spelled out are two very different things. That email landed hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I told myself I'd just have one drink to take the edge off and then get back to it. And then I woke up at like 2am on the couch with the laptop still open and an empty bottle next to me. And the document was just... blank. I'd written nothing. So that was fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still got yourself here today after a week like that — I don't take that lightly. I want to ask you something, and take your time with it. When you think about your actual research, not the deadlines, not your advisor — what does it mean to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... that's the thing, right? Like I actually care about this stuff. The work I'm doing on language development in bilingual kids — there are real families out there. Real kids. And when I'm... when I'm actually in it and I'm sober and focused, I feel like I'm supposed to be doing this. But then the other part of my brain just keeps going, what if everyone's been wrong about you? What if you got in here by accident and they're about to figure that out?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this version of you — the researcher who genuinely cares about those kids and their families, who feels like this work is his. And then there's the 2am version, waking up on the couch, convinced he's a fraud. Both of those feel real right now. And somewhere in the middle, the drinking started out as a way to get through the day... but it's starting to get in the way of the thing you actually want.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. When you put it like that. I've been telling myself the stress is the problem and the drinking is just like, a symptom or whatever. But I missed a meeting with my advisor last week because I felt too foggy to string a sentence together. That's not stress doing that. That's — that's me doing that to myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing to say out loud. What do you think it might look like, a few months from now, if things started moving in a different direction?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... actually sleeping? Being able to read a paper without re-reading the same paragraph like six times. Showing up to my advisor's office without that constant low-level dread. I used to really love my work. Like there were nights I'd look up and it was midnight and I hadn't even noticed. I want — I think I want that back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That picture you just described — that's not vague. That's specific, and it's yours. You came in here today after one of the harder weeks you've had, and instead of defending where things are, you told me what you actually want. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I've been so scared of failing that I forgot what it felt like to actually try. But... yeah. I think I'm ready to do something different. I don't know exactly what yet, but — yeah.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I wasn't sure you would, honestly. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My parents basically dragged me here again so. Not like I had a choice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sure. And still — you're in the seat. Last week you barely said ten words. What's different today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Nothing's different. I mean... I just— they won't stop fighting about it at home. Like every single night now. So whatever, I'm here, I'm talking. Doesn't mean I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fighting at home is getting to you. Every night sounds exhausting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... yeah. It is. My dad barely looks at me anymore and my mom just cries and I'm just— I don't know. I didn't think it was gonna be this big of a deal. It was just some beers, it's not like I was— I don't know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't expect it to blow up the way it did. And now you're watching your dad check out and your mom break down, and somewhere underneath all that tough "whatever" — I'm thinking you're actually pretty scared.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I'm not scared. I just— okay, fine. Maybe a little. But it's not about the drinking, it's about them overreacting. Right? Like I made one mistake and now my whole house is falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Help me understand the "one mistake" part. Because you hid bottles in your room — that's not a one-night thing. What was going on when you started doing that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay it was more than once. I know. I'm not stupid. It was like— school's been really bad this year and my friend group kind of exploded and I just... it helped me stop thinking for a while. That's it. It wasn't like an addiction thing or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm hearing you right. School got really hard, you lost people you were close to, and drinking was the one thing that shut the noise off for a bit. That makes sense to me. I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. And at the same time — you're sixteen, hiding bottles, your family's falling apart, and you just told me it was more than once. What does that add up to for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. Maybe it got kind of out of hand. I didn't— I kept telling myself I'd stop but then stuff kept happening and it was just easier to not deal with it that way. And now I'm here and my dad won't look at me and I just... I don't want things to stay like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's the first time you've said what you actually want. "I don't want things to stay like this." That matters. What would it mean to you if things actually got better — with your dad, with school, with all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just want him to look at me like he used to. Like before all this. And I want to actually... I don't know, feel okay without needing something to make me feel okay. Is that weird to say?

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — your friend set this up, from what I understand. I'm curious, what's your take on being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, Dave basically wouldn't let it go until I made the appointment. Look, I'll be straight with you — I don't think I have a problem. Guys drink. We all drank over there. You come back, you decompress, that's just... that's how it works in the military. Always has been. I don't see why everybody's suddenly treating it like it's some big thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking's been part of the fabric of military life for as long as you've been in it. It's not something you ever thought twice about — until other people started making it an issue.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm some guy cracking a beer at eight in the morning, you know? I hold down a job. I show up. Most days I'm... I'm fine. I have a few beers at night, maybe more on weekends. But that's normal. Half the guys I served with do the same thing. Nobody's dragging them to a VA clinic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "Most days." I noticed that. When you think about what's actually on the line for you right now — what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. My wife, I guess. She... she gave me an ultimatum. Said she'd leave. Take the kids. And part of me keeps saying she doesn't get it, she doesn't understand what it was like over there. But then... the other night she was just sitting at the kitchen table crying and I — I didn't know what to do. I just stood there. That's not me. I used to know how to be there for people. I was good at that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment sticks with you. Her at the table, and you standing there feeling like you'd lost access to the part of yourself that knew how to reach her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I'm not ready to say drinking is the whole problem. There's a lot of other stuff going on. But she keeps saying I'm not present. Like I'm physically there but I'm... somewhere else. And I hate that she's right about that. I actually hate it. That's not the kind of husband I thought I'd be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm tracking this right. You came in because Dave pushed you, not because you'd decided you had a problem. And at the same time — your wife is at her limit, and instead of being able to shake that off, something about it gets through. You can see yourself in what she's describing. And underneath all of it, there's this guy who used to know how to show up, who valued being that person, and who's not sure where he went.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — I haven't really put it together like that before. I'm not making any promises or whatever. But maybe I've been telling myself things are fine and just... not looking too hard at what's underneath that. Maybe for a while now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to actually sit with that instead of just moving on. A lot of people don't. You're still here, and you're not pretending you didn't just say what you said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my family. That's — that's the bottom line, right there. I don't know exactly what any of this looks like yet. But I think I want to figure it out. Like, actually try. For once.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... you're here. Before we get into anything — I just want to say, I'm glad you showed up today. That matters. What's going on for you right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really want to be here. My boss basically said 'go talk to someone or we're having a very different conversation,' so... here I am. I'm not — I don't think I have like, some big problem. I had one bad night. One.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like this whole thing got put on you. Like the decision to be here wasn't really yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. I mean... look, I bartend. I get home at 2, sometimes 3 in the morning. I have a couple drinks to wind down, decompress, whatever. That's just — that's the industry. Everyone does it. It's not like I'm drinking on the job or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like when you tried to remember the last day you didn't drink... and couldn't?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — it wasn't like some big dramatic moment. Someone just asked me offhand and I couldn't answer and it... pissed me off, to be honest. Like why does that matter? I show up, I do my job, I'm functioning. Most days I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "Most days." ... You said that and then kind of let it hang there. I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I don't know. That night at work — I wasn't sloshed or anything, I just was... off. I dropped something, said something to a customer I shouldn't have. And I keep telling myself it was just fatigue, long week, whatever. But like... I don't know. Maybe. I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's the part of this that you don't want to look at?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...That maybe it's not the fatigue. Like maybe I've just been running on fumes and alcohol for so long that I don't even know what normal feels like anymore. And I'm 27. That's — I mean, that's a weird thing to realize about yourself at 27.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today feeling pushed into this room, like it wasn't your choice. And somewhere in this conversation, without really meaning to, you said something true — that you might not know what normal feels like anymore. That took courage to say. What would it mean for you, to find that out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think it would mean a lot, actually. It's kind of messed up because my whole job is helping people feel good for a few hours, right? Like, forget it all. And I've just been doing the same thing to myself. Every night. I don't know what I want yet but I think I actually need to figure that out.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you. It's been a few weeks... last time you were in, you mentioned things had been feeling a little different. More like you had some footing. How have things been going since then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... okay. It's been okay. Had a rough patch, whatever, but I'm not here to — I don't know, I'm not falling apart or anything. The doctor thing was probably nothing. They always blow everything out of proportion, you know? You go in for a routine thing and suddenly they're acting like you're dying. I've seen guys in way worse shape than me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. You're holding onto the idea that it's probably nothing... and at the same time, something brought you back in here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah, I came back. I said I would. I keep my word. That's... look, the numbers were off, the liver stuff. The doc said to cut back. I've been cutting back. I went three days last week without a drink, so. I don't know what else they want from me. Three days. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three days. That's real. That took something from you — I don't want to gloss over that. And I'm also sitting here noticing... you said the numbers were off, and the way you said it, there was something underneath that. What was that like, getting that news?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was — I don't know. Whatever. I wasn't scared if that's what you're asking. I've had way scarier days. You want scared? I'll tell you about scared. This is... this is just numbers on a piece of paper. The thing that pissed me off is everyone acting like I have a problem. Sarah forwarded me the appointment summary like I'm some kind of — like I can't handle my own medical stuff. Like I'm fragile. I'm not fragile.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
She forwarded it to you... 

...

What do you make of that? Why do you think she did that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
Because she's... 

...

She's scared. I know she's scared. She doesn't say it like that, she says it angry, but I know what that is. We've been married eleven years. I know what her scared looks like. And I just — I can't be the reason she looks like that. I hate that I'm the reason she looks like that. She didn't sign up for this, you know? She signed up for — I don't even know what she signed up for. Not this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You love her. And right now you're carrying the weight of knowing that what you've been doing is hurting her, hurting yourself... and you're also a man who went three days without drinking last week because some part of you is fighting for something. For her maybe. For yourself. I'm not sure yet — maybe you're not either.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
She said... she said if nothing changes by summer, she's taking Mia and going to her mom's. And I thought — I thought I had more time. I thought I was managing it. I served two tours, I came home, I'm still here, I'm still showing up. But showing up half-present, that's... that's not really showing up, is it. 

...

I don't want to lose them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
That just landed. 

...

You said showing up half-present isn't really showing up. Where does that thought come from?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
From... I don't know, from watching my own dad do it. He was there. Physically there. But he wasn't — he was somewhere else. And I swore I wasn't gonna be that. I swore it. 

...

Maybe I can actually do this differently. I don't know how yet. But maybe — maybe that's something we can figure out. I'm not saying it's gonna be easy. I'm just saying I'm not ready to stop trying.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this kind of appointment isn't always easy to show up to. Can you tell me, in your own words, what's been going on lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm only here because my partner basically gave me an ultimatum. Like, said they'd leave if I didn't come talk to someone. So... here I am. I don't think I have some huge problem, I really don't. It's just - things have been a lot lately and I have a glass of wine at night to unwind. That's it. I mean, I work full time, I've got two kids, there's no one else helping. I think that's pretty... normal, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the pressure to be here came from outside - from your partner - not really from you. And the wine is doing something important at the end of the day. It's giving you a way to decompress when there's nothing left.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, nobody gets it unless they're doing what I'm doing. I wake up at six, I get two kids out the door, I work eight hours, I pick them up, I make dinner, I do homework, I do baths, I do bedtime - and by nine o'clock I am just... done. Empty. And yeah, I have a bottle of wine over the course of the night and it helps me shut my brain off enough to actually sleep. I don't see why that's a crisis.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word you used - empty. What does that actually feel like for you, at the end of those days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... um. It's lonely, honestly. I didn't expect to be doing all of this by myself. I love my kids, I do, but they need everything from me all the time and there's no one who's... checking on me, you know? So I pour that first glass and it's like the only twenty minutes in the whole day where I'm not somebody's mom or somebody's employee or somebody's problem. I'm just... nothing. Which sounds terrible but it's actually a relief. And I know that sounds bad. I know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound bad - it sounds like someone who is completely depleted and found the one thing that gives her five minutes of peace. You're carrying a tremendous amount alone. And I noticed you said 'I know' twice there, like there's a part of you that's already having a different conversation with yourself about this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My daughter asked me last week why I always smell like wine when I tuck her in at night. She's nine. She wasn't being mean about it, she was just - asking. Like it was a normal question. And I laughed it off but I haven't stopped thinking about it since then. I don't want that to be her memory of me. I don't want her to grow up and look back and think that's just... who her mom was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's a lot here. You're exhausted in a way that goes bone-deep - doing this alone, no backup, no one filling your cup back up. The wine became a way to survive that. And now your partner is worried enough to issue an ultimatum, and your daughter is noticing. But the thing underneath all of it - the thing that seems to actually matter to you - is the mom you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... you got it. I'm not trying to be this person. I think somewhere along the way I just started surviving instead of actually living and I... I don't want to keep doing that. I think I'd like to figure out something different. I don't know what, but... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Surviving versus actually living. That's a real distinction. What would actually living start to look like for you - even something small?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not just waiting for the kids to go to sleep so I can drink. Maybe having enough left in me to actually sit with my daughter for a few minutes before bed instead of just going through the motions. I've been doing bedtime on autopilot for months. God, saying it out loud is... okay. Yeah. I think I'm actually ready to try something different. Like for real, not just because my partner made me come here.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey. I know you've got somewhere to be after this, so I don't want to waste your time. You showed up, which - I want you to know I don't take that lightly. What would make this hour actually worth something for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Nothing. Look, my buddy Derek - he basically ambushed me last week. Sat me down with this whole... intervention thing, like I'm some kind of... I don't know. I'm here because he wouldn't let it go. That's it. I don't actually think there's a problem here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this wasn't your call. Someone you care about pushed you through that door, and part of you is - I'm guessing - pretty pissed off about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm pissed. Derek never deployed. He doesn't get it. You go over there, you see what we saw, come back and - look, everyone drinks. It's how you decompress, how you stay sane. My whole unit, same exact thing. It's not a problem, it's just... it's military life. It's what you do. And now I'm sitting in a counselor's office at a college because my buddy decided to play doctor.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You built a way of surviving over there. Drinking, being with your guys - that wasn't weakness, that was the culture, that was how you got through it. And now someone's slapping a label on it, and it feels like... like they're calling you broken without ever having been where you were.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Nobody gets it. And I'm - I'm functioning. I go to school, I show up, I'm not some... I'm not falling apart. My wife, she's - she's got this whole thing where she thinks... I don't know. She's been making noises about leaving and I think that's what set Derek off. But she doesn't understand the pressure either. Nobody does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot. School, whatever's still with you from over there, and now your marriage feeling like it's... cracking. And you're still showing up to all of it. That matters... What happens inside you when you think about actually losing her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't want to lose her. I mean - we have a kid. My son is four years old. And she said it last month, she actually used the word divorce, out loud, and I just kind of... I brushed it off. But then it's like three in the morning and I can't sleep and I'm sitting there thinking - what if she means it? What if I'm actually... what if I'm screwing everything up and I can't even see it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That three in the morning voice... it's asking questions you can't afford to look at in the daylight. And I wonder - I just wonder - if part of what makes this room feel so wrong is that sitting here means maybe taking that voice seriously.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Maybe. I'm not - I'm not ready to say I'm an alcoholic or whatever. I don't think that's what this is. But I also... I don't want my son growing up thinking his dad is... you know. I don't want that to be who I am to him. My own dad had a thing with - anyway. I just. I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of this for a second, because I think it matters. You came in here because Derek pushed you - not because you believe there's a problem, and some part of you still doesn't. And at the same time there's your wife saying the word divorce, there's your son, there's your own father somewhere in the background, and there's that voice at three in the morning you can't shake. You're not ready to call it anything. But you're also saying you're not willing to lose your family.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... No. No, I'm not. I don't know where I'd even - like I don't know what any of this looks like. But no. I survived two deployments. I'm not gonna let this be the thing that takes everything down. I can't lose my family. So... yeah. I don't know. But no.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, welcome in — glad you found us. And I mean that literally, because parking on this street is basically its own trauma. So, what brings you in today? What made today the day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. I just finished a detox program. Last week. They said I should, you know, follow up with someone. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. So this was more... following through on something that was recommended, not necessarily something you felt like you needed right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — I know I was drinking too much. Obviously. But I've been under a lot of stress. Like, a lot. I'm raising two kids by myself, I work full-time, there's nobody helping me. So it's not like I was just doing it for fun or whatever. It was... it was how I got through the nights.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes complete sense. A bottle of wine at the end of the day stops feeling like drinking and starts feeling like just... surviving. And surviving two kids solo while working full-time — that's not nothing. I'm curious though, something made you look up that detox program in the first place. What shifted?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter said something. She's twelve. She... she told me she was scared to wake me up in the mornings because she never knew if I was going to be okay. And I just — that hit different, you know? Like I kept telling myself I was holding everything together for them, and then she said that and I couldn't... I just couldn't argue with it anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She showed you something you couldn't unsee. And you listened. I don't want to gloss over that — a lot of people would've shut that down or gotten really defensive. You didn't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I cried for like two days. Then I looked it up. I just... I don't want her to be scared of me. That's not who I want to be. I got so exhausted and I didn't know what else to do, I didn't have any other — I don't know. I didn't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm tracking all of this. You've been carrying a massive load — single parenting, no real support, full-time work — and the wine became the only thing that made the nights feel manageable. Then your daughter said something that cracked that open. And instead of shutting down, you found a detox program, you went through it, and now you're sitting here a week later. That's a lot of movement in a short time. So when you picture things six months from now — what do you want that to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be... present. Like actually there. Not just physically in the room but already half-checked-out by eight o'clock. I want to be someone she's not scared of. And honestly? I want to sleep. Real sleep. I haven't slept right in years and I didn't even realize it until last week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present, being someone she trusts, getting actual rest — those aren't small things. That's a really clear picture of what matters to you. And it sounds like part of you already knows the direction. So what feels like the most doable next step, just from here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... keeping the appointments, I think. Showing up. I'm really good at canceling when things get overwhelming. But I showed up today, so. Maybe that counts for something.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to see you again. Come in, sit wherever feels comfortable... I heard from your sister that this past week was a rough one. I just want to start by checking in — how are you feeling right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I didn't even want to come. My sister, she — she basically dragged me here. I'm fine. I mean, yes, I drank a little more this week, but it's not like... she acts like I'm some kind of alcoholic or something. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is really frustrated to be here — like this wasn't your choice, and maybe it feels like your sister is exaggerating what's going on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. She doesn't even live here, you know? She calls me from back home, she's like, 'you have a problem,' and I'm thinking — you have no idea what it's like here. She has her husband, her friends, her whole life. I'm here alone. I drink a little to... to get through the evenings. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying something really heavy — being far from everyone you love, no one nearby who really understands. What was this past week like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. It was just... bad. Um. There was this thing at work where my manager, she said something in front of everyone and I couldn't — I didn't understand the reference, it was some cultural thing, and everyone laughed and I just felt so... so stupid. So small. And then I went home and the apartment was quiet and I thought, okay, just one glass. But then it was the whole bottle. And then I called my sister crying, which is why she called you, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment at work — feeling invisible, like you couldn't quite belong — and then coming home to that silence... it sounds like the drinking felt like the only way to soften that kind of pain.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, it did. For like an hour it did. And then I just felt worse. And ashamed. I kept thinking, what am I even doing here? I left everything for — for what? And I know drinking isn't the answer, I know that. I'm not stupid. I just... I don't know what else to do when it gets like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet — even in that moment — you knew it wasn't helping. And you still picked up the phone and called your sister. That took something. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I guess. I never thought of it that way. I usually just feel embarrassed about that call. Like, why can't I just handle things? But maybe... maybe reaching out was okay. I don't know. I think what scares me is that there's no one here to call before it gets that bad. Like, I need something — someone — before the bottle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what I'm hearing is — underneath all of this, there's a deep longing for connection. And the part of you that called your sister, the part that walked in here today even though you really didn't want to... that part is already reaching out. Already looking for something different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, I think so. I never really said that out loud before. It's not about the alcohol, is it. It's about being so... alone. I want to figure out how to not feel like that anymore. I don't know how, but... I think I want to try.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, appreciate you logging on. Fair warning — I've got a dog that may or may not lose her mind at some point and I'm just gonna pretend it didn't happen. So. Welcome to 2026 therapy. How you doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here. That's about all I got for you. My buddy basically wouldn't shut the hell up until I made this appointment, so. Don't take it personal, but I don't really think I need to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your buddy has one read on things. You've got another. What's the gap look like from where you're sitting?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: His read is I drink too much. My read is he's never been downrange so he can keep his opinions to himself. Look — I did two tours. You know what we did after missions? We drank. Every single one of us. That's just... that's how it works over there, and that's how it works when you get back. It's not like I'm some guy falling down in a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking was never a problem — it was the solution. The way guys stayed sane, stayed connected. And now somebody who wasn't there is telling you there's something wrong with it. That'd piss me off too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. Nobody gets it. I got guys I served with, we all drink like this, none of them are sitting in front of some... no offense. Look, I function. I go to work, I pay my bills. I'm not a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'I go to work, I pay my bills' — and then you kind of stopped. What happens after that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I come home and I... I unwind. Have a few beers. Maybe more than a few, I don't know. My wife, she's got a whole different take on it. She thinks... she wants me to be some version of me that just doesn't exist anymore. I can't explain it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's watching you and she's scared. And some part of you already knows that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She, uh... she said if things don't change she's taking the kids and going to her mom's. And I hear myself saying I'm fine, but... I don't want that. I don't want my kids growing up without me in the house. That's not — that's not what I came back for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm tracking you. You came in because your buddy pushed you, and part of you was ready to push right back out the door. The drinking made sense — it still makes sense to you, it's woven into who you are and what you've been through. And at the same time, there's this other thing sitting right underneath all of it: your wife drawing a line, your kids in the picture, and this quiet fear that 'I'm fine' might end up costing you the people you actually care about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I don't know what to do with that yet. But that's the thing that keeps me up at night. Not the — not any of this. Just... I don't want to lose my family.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you again. I know this week was a hard one... how are you feeling right now, just sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Rough, I guess. I... yeah. I kind of went backwards this week. Like, I had told myself I was gonna try to cut back, and then Thursday happened and I just... didn't. Didn't even try, really.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So Thursday really knocked you off course. And it sounds like there was some part of you that genuinely wanted to do things differently — that intention was real — and then something got in the way of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It was a brutal shift, like three bachelorette parties back to back, you know? And when I got home it was like... I couldn't not have a drink. Or five. And then I woke up the next morning and I just felt — I don't know. Disgusted, kind of. With myself. Which doesn't usually happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word — disgusted — that's a heavy thing to wake up feeling. What was going through your mind in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I kept thinking about what Marco said at the intervention thing. That he hadn't seen me actually sober in like two years. And I sat there in my kitchen and I tried to think of the last time I wasn't drinking and I... I couldn't come up with one. Not one day. And I thought — what's the point, you know? Like this is just who I am now. This is just my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's such a painful place to land — feeling like there's no space between you and this thing, like it's just become who you are.
