I want to stay with that for a moment... and I also want to notice something. You said Marco's words stayed with you all week. They didn't just slide off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Marco's been my best friend since high school. He's not — he's not a dramatic guy, you know what I mean? For him to actually do that, to get people together like that... I keep seeing his face when he said it. He looked scared. Like, actually scared. For me. And that's been eating at me all week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that it was Marco — someone who knows you, who isn't prone to making a big deal out of things — and he looked scared. That landed in a way it might not have if it came from someone else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And I've been thinking like... I don't want to be the person people worry about. I don't want Marco looking at me like that. I want to — I don't know, I think I actually want to try. For real this time. Not just say it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted in you this week. Even with everything that happened — Thursday, the hard shift, the setback — you still came back here today. And now you're sitting here telling me you want to try for real. That's not a small thing. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's weird, I came in here feeling like such a failure. But... maybe Thursday doesn't cancel everything out? I don't know. I just — I don't want to keep waking up and not being able to remember the last sober day. That's not... that's not the life I want for myself.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know that first call can be the hardest part. I don't have any agenda today — I'm just curious, what was it that actually made you pick up the phone?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly, my doctor kind of freaked me out. My liver enzymes came back elevated, which — okay, I Googled it immediately and apparently that can mean like a million different things, so. But she kept pushing, asking all these questions, and I was like... I don't know. I figured maybe I should just talk to someone so I could go back and tell her I'm handling it. I feel completely fine, though. Like, I do SoulCycle four times a week. My skin is great. I just posted a wellness reel last Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your body sent a signal that caught you off guard — and at the same time, everything else you see and feel tells you that you're doing fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And like — okay, she asked specifically about drinking, and I get it, that's the obvious thing to ask, but... I'm in hospitality content. That is literally my career. I go to openings, I do brand partnerships with wine labels, I fly to Napa for press trips. You can't just separate that out. If I stopped drinking I would lose — I mean, it would be like a chef saying they can't taste food anymore. It's not... *laughs nervously* ...it's not comparable to some guy drinking alone in his apartment, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like drinking is really threaded through your work, your identity, how people know you. I want to ask you something a little different though — has anyone in your personal life, someone who isn't your doctor, said anything to you about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My sister, but she doesn't drink at all so she's always been like that. I kind of tune her out, honestly. And... *pauses* ...my best friend Kyla texted me after my birthday last month. She said she was worried. Which — I mean, it was my birthday, we were all drunk, so that felt a little rich coming from her. But Kyla's not the type to say stuff like that for no reason. She doesn't do drama. She just... she said she'd been watching me and she was scared. And I just like, didn't respond for three days. I still haven't really responded. *looks at hands* I don't know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You brushed it off — but you remember exactly what she said. And you're still sitting with it three weeks later.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's been my best friend since sophomore year of college. So yeah, it's not like I can just... I don't know. But I also genuinely think people project. Like I'm not — I go to beautiful places and I document my life and people love it. That is not the same as having a problem. I did Dry January last year. Mostly. The last week I kind of... but I did it. I'm capable of stopping. I just choose not to because it's my job and also because I like it and there's nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got a lot of things landing at once — your body signaling something, Kyla saying something out of character, and still you showed up here today. I'm curious — and you don't have to have an answer — what would you want your life to actually look like five years from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to still be doing this. I love what I do, genuinely. I want to still have the energy for it, not be running on fumes by like three in the afternoon. And I want... *quiet for a moment* ...I want to be the kind of person Kyla doesn't have to worry about. I know that sounds weird after everything I just said. I hear myself. But yeah. That's what I actually want.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I've heard today. You came in because a lab result unsettled you enough that you couldn't fully dismiss it. You have a career and a whole world that you love, and it's deeply tied to drinking — and that makes this feel really complicated, not simple. And someone who has known you for over a decade, who doesn't do drama, told you she was scared. That landed. Underneath all of it, there's someone who wants to keep doing what she loves, wants to feel like herself, and wants to be okay — for herself, and for Kyla. That's not a small thing to walk in here carrying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. *exhales* I'm not committing to anything crazy, just so we're clear. I'm not about to become someone who posts about mocktails. *small laugh* But maybe I don't have to have it all figured out right now. Can we just — can we start from here? Is that allowed?

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back. I know last time felt... a little uncertain, maybe. It takes something to walk through that door a second time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... I almost didn't, honestly. I sat in my car for like fifteen minutes. But the doctor called again about my results and I just — I don't know. I figured I should at least come back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about that call pushed you back here, even when part of you wanted to drive away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... the labs. They said my liver numbers are off. And I kept thinking, it's probably nothing, right? Like I'm twenty-nine, things like that don't happen at twenty-nine. But then I couldn't sleep and I kept — I don't know. What if it's not nothing?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear crept in when you least expected it. I'm wondering — when you're lying awake with that worry... what else is there? What does that 3am feel like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... quiet. Too quiet. Back home there was always someone — my mom in the next room, cousins calling, just... noise. Here I come home and it's nothing. Just me. And I started drinking because at least it made the quiet feel less — I don't know how to explain it. Less sharp, I guess. Like it takes the edge off the loneliness.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking became a way to soften something that's actually really painful — being so far from everyone who knows you. That's not a small thing to carry alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No one really gets it here. People are nice but it's like... surface level, you know? And I don't want to complain because I chose to come here, I was supposed to build something. But sometimes I feel like I made a mistake and the drinking is — I know it's not good. I think I knew that before the labs. I just didn't want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came here to build something — and that dream is still in you. What would it mean if things were different? If the quiet didn't feel so sharp?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'd actually want to meet people. Like really try. There's a group at the cultural center I keep seeing flyers for but I always talk myself out of it. Maybe that's stupid. But yeah — I think I want to feel like I belong somewhere again. Even just a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to bring this together. You sat in your car today and almost left — but you didn't. You've been carrying a lot of loneliness, and drinking has been how you've managed that quiet. Now your body is sending a signal you can't ignore. And at the same time, there's this part of you that still has a vision — connection, belonging, building something real. That part showed up here today too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. I didn't think about it that way but — I didn't leave. I'm here. Maybe that means something.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. I want to say — I know last time wasn't exactly comfortable, and you still came back. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha — yeah, well. My 11 o'clock cancelled, so. Timing worked out. I'm not like, committed to this or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Noted. No commitments. So — what's the week looked like? What's been going on since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Good, honestly. Really good. I did this collab dinner Friday and it got like forty thousand impressions, which for a weeknight thing is insane. And I'm in talks with a new spirits brand, which is just... *laughs* I mean, people keep paying me to do exactly what I was already doing, so. Hard to see the problem, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So professionally things are moving and in a lot of ways the life you've built feels like it's working. ... You mentioned last week that a couple of your friends had said something — about your drinking. I'm wondering if any of that crossed your mind this week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... Jess has always been dramatic, so I kind of take what she says with a grain of salt. And Maya — Maya's been sober for like two years, so everything gets filtered through that lens for her, you know? I love them both but they're not living my life. They don't know what my life actually requires. I thought about it for like five minutes and then I had a shoot to prep for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You pushed it aside — but it did come up. And Jess, Maya... these aren't strangers. These are people you're close to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I know that. *quieter* It's just... I don't know how to explain to them that this isn't — it's not what they think it is. Like yes, I drink, a lot of people drink, my whole world drinks. That's not the same as having a problem. I just... I don't love that they see me that way. It's like they're waiting for me to fall apart. And I'm just not falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm tracking this right. You've built something real — a platform, a career, a lifestyle that feels genuinely yours. And at the same time, people you trust are saying something's off, and you're not entirely dismissing them, even while you push back. And underneath all of it, something about how they see you... bothers you. Like they're watching for you to be someone you don't think you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... *long pause* Yeah. I mean — *laughs softly* — I don't even know why that landed like that. It's fine. I'm fine. But like... yeah. Sometimes I think about what it would be like to just not have everything be a whole thing, you know? Show up somewhere and not have to be Dani, like the whole brand of it. But that's burnout. That's not a me-and-alcohol situation, that's just — this industry is a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would that look like — a version of your life where you're not always 'on'?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: *exhales* I mean — I'm not going sober, I want to be really clear about that. *laughs* But I guess... maybe sometimes quieter? Like there's this version of Saturday mornings I used to have where I'd just make coffee and read, and that was it. I haven't done that in... I can't even remember. *pause* Maybe there's something in there. I don't know. I'm not saying anything's wrong. I'm just — yeah. Maybe.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this maybe wasn't how you were planning to spend your morning, so... I just want you to know there's no agenda here. No checklist. We can just talk. How are you feeling right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I mean, I'm here because my coach basically told me I had to be, said if I didn't show up he'd pull my playing time, maybe my scholarship. So. Yeah. I don't think I have a problem. I party like every other guy on the team. This whole thing is just... it's blown way out of proportion and nobody wants to hear that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this feels like something that was done to you. Like you got pulled into a room and handed an ultimatum, and now you're sitting here... and it doesn't feel fair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, I've been busting my ass for this team for two years. Two years. And I have one bad stretch and suddenly I'm — what, some kind of addict? That's not me. That's not who I am. My coach doesn't even know what goes on in the locker room, he just picks on me because I'm visible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two years of putting in that work — that's real. And it sounds like being an athlete, being someone your team counts on, that's not just what you do. That's kind of who you are. And yet you're here. Even when a big part of you didn't want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. Look, it's just — my boys, the team, going out after wins, that's my whole social life. I'm not gonna become some monk who doesn't hang out just because... I don't know. I just don't want to lose that. Those are my people. And I already did the detox thing, okay? I did what they asked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those friendships clearly mean a lot. And so does your place on that team. I'm curious about something, and take your time with this — when you picture yourself a few years from now, what does that look like? What do you actually want?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I used to know. Like, the draft was something I actually thought about seriously. Scouts came to two of our games last season. But lately my times are down, my numbers are off, and I'm just... I finished the detox and I feel okay but I'm like — what if it's already too late? What if I already messed it up?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're scared that the version of you who had that future — the draft, the performance — might be harder to get back than you'd like. And at the same time... that future still means something to you. You haven't let go of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it does. I still want it. Like, I worked too hard. My mom drove four hours every single weekend in high school just to watch me play. Four hours. And I just... I don't want to look back and know I threw that away for — for what. I just don't know how to separate it all. The drinking from the hangouts, the team stuff, all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I'm getting it right. You walked in today feeling like you didn't have a choice, like this was unfair. And underneath all of that, there's something you care about deeply — your team, your friendships, a sport you've built your whole life around. And when you look ahead, there's still a version of the future you want. A future your mom drove four hours to be part of. And what you're trying to figure out is how to hold onto all of that... without losing the people who matter to you along the way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's it. I've never actually said any of that out loud before. I think I do want to figure this out. I just needed to know someone actually wanted to listen. Not just, like, fix me or tell me what to do.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, glad you made it in. I know this probably wasn't exactly at the top of your to-do list today — right up there with, I don't know, a trip to the DMV maybe. I'm just going to say upfront, this isn't a place where I'm going to lecture you or tell you what to do. So — what would you want me to know about why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here because my school basically made me. Like, my counselor said it was this or some kind of disciplinary thing, so. I don't even really think it's a big deal. Everyone drinks. Literally everyone at that party was drinking, I just got caught and now I'm the one who has to do all this. It's kind of... I don't know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it feels like you got unlucky — like you were doing what everybody else was doing and somehow you're the one sitting here holding the bag for it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. It's not like I have some... problem or whatever. I had a few drinks. That's it. I'm not like... I'm not an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes sense, feeling that way. Can I ask you about something though? You just came out of detox — like, that's not a small thing. What was that actually like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I don't know. Weird. I didn't think it was going to be that intense, honestly. Like I always thought detox was for — I don't know — like older people who've been drinking for years. Not me. And then the doctor told me my BAC when I came in and I was like... okay that number is kind of scary. But I still think it got way blown out of proportion by everyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is still saying 'this is too much, I don't belong here' — and then another part of you heard that number and got a little spooked.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Kind of. I don't remember everything from that night and that's... I don't know, that's a little messed up actually. I just — I really don't want to be like, the girl with the drinking problem. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you're even letting yourself say that out loud — 'I don't want this to become a thing' — that actually takes a lot of self-awareness. A lot of people at your stage don't go there at all.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about it more since detox, like... why did I drink that much? I keep going back to that. It wasn't even fun at a certain point, I just — I don't know. I think I was trying to keep up? Or not look like I was scared? I'm not even sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just pull this together for a second — you came in today feeling like the whole thing was unfair, like you got caught doing what everyone does. And at the same time, something about detox shook you. You heard a number that scared you, you've got gaps in the night you can't fill in. And now you're sitting with this question that actually matters a lot: why that much, and why keep going when it stopped being fun. That question you're asking yourself? That's exactly the right place to start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess I never really thought about it like that before, but... yeah. That's kind of what's been in my head.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this wasn't exactly your idea. What made you decide to walk through that door?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My husband gave me an ultimatum. He said if I didn't come here he was going to leave, so... here I am. I don't think I actually have a problem. But apparently everyone else has decided that for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So right now this is more about keeping your marriage together than anything you feel like you need for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. I mean... look, I drink sometimes. So what? I moved to this country alone. My English was not even good when I came. I didn't know anybody. You try living like that — waking up every day and having nobody, not one person, to just... talk to. Drinking makes it easier. It's not like I'm — I'm not some drunk.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what it's actually been like — being here with no one around.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you want me to say? That it's lonely? Fine. Yes. It's lonely. I left everything — my mom, my sisters, my friends, my whole life. And my husband, he works, like, always, so I come home to this... empty apartment. Every single day. And I drink. Okay? It helps me sleep. It helps me stop thinking about how isolated I am. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It took real courage to uproot your entire life and start over somewhere you didn't even know the language. And what you figured out — using alcohol to get through the nights, to quiet all of that — it made sense. It worked, at least for a while.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I guess. But now he's saying it's too much and I don't know, maybe I do drink more than before. A little. But what am I supposed to do instead? I can't just sit there. I can't talk to nobody forever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you can't talk to nobody forever. What would it actually mean for you — to have someone here to talk to?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know, I've never really let myself think about it. Back home I had my sisters. We talked every day. Here it's just texts, and the time difference, and it's not... it's not the same. If I had even one real person here... um... maybe I wouldn't need the wine every night. Maybe. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm hearing you right. You didn't come here today because you believe you have a problem. You came because the person you love is scared, and you didn't want to lose him. But somewhere in this conversation, something else showed up — this image of what your life could look like if you actually had connection here. Real connection. And the possibility that maybe you wouldn't need alcohol to survive the nights. That part — that's not your husband's. That's yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's right. I just want to feel like a person again. Not like someone who's just... getting through the day. If that's something I could actually have here, then... maybe it's worth trying for.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to walk through that door, especially when you've done this before and it didn't quite land the way you hoped. I'm glad you're here. So... what's on your mind coming in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly, I'm here because my colleague basically made it impossible not to be. She pulled me aside and... look, she wasn't wrong that I wasn't at my best that morning, but she made it into this whole thing. Called it a pattern. I mean, I've been teaching for eleven years. I think I'd know if I had a pattern.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So someone you work with noticed something, and that pushed this into motion - and part of you is still kind of sitting with whether you even agreed with her read on things.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And I've done counseling twice before, so it's not like I'm... resistant to the idea or whatever. It just, um, didn't really do anything either time. I drink in the evenings. I wind down, I get up, I go teach. I'm not missing days. I'm not showing up slurring. That morning I was just a little tired, and she blew it up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm curious about the evenings. When you pour that drink after work... what does it actually do for you? What does it give you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... it's the only time the noise stops. Middle schoolers are a lot. They need things from you constantly, all day. And when I get home and I have that first drink, there's this... exhale. You know? Everything just gets quieter. I don't know, maybe that sounds like an excuse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound like an excuse. It sounds like you've found something that genuinely works - that gives you real relief after a genuinely hard day. And I want to say, the honesty in that answer... that's not nothing. A lot of people can't go there that quickly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Yeah, it works. But - okay, I'll be honest. The mornings have been harder. Like I used to just bounce back, and now I'm standing in front of thirty kids hoping they can't tell I'm not all there. And that's... that bothers me more than I want it to. I care about those kids.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what I'm hearing is - the evenings matter, they give you something real that you need. And the mornings are starting to cost you something. And the thing that you keep coming back to... is those kids. That you show up for them. That's who you are as a teacher. It sounds like there's a part of you that's been quietly noticing for a while that something is shifting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I guess there is. I just - I've always been the one who has it together, you know? I'm the guy colleagues come to when they're struggling. Being on this side of it feels... weird. But maybe I've been telling myself things are fine for longer than they actually have been.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you to keep looking at this honestly - the way you just did right now, in this room?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know yet. Maybe... maybe something different than the other times. Because those times I wasn't really - I was going through the motions. Right now I'm actually talking. That's, um... that's at least something, I think.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. [pause] I just want to say — that's not nothing. A lot of people don't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. [exhales] I don't really know why I'm here again, honestly. My buddy keeps getting on my case about it and I figured... whatever. Don't make it into a whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like pressure. Like people around you have already decided something about you, and now you're here because of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like I'm not — I'm not some kind of... I work in a bar. Everyone drinks. That's just what you do after a shift, you decompress, you talk shit with the crew. Nobody else is out here making it into this huge crisis, you know? It's like, why am I the one who has to sit in a therapist's office?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet... something brought you back here today. What was going through your mind when you were deciding whether to come?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... [long pause] ...there was this moment last week. I was trying to think of, like, when did I last not drink? And I just — I couldn't. I kept going back through the days and I couldn't find one. And that kind of... I don't know, it stuck with me. I'm not saying it's a big deal, but it stuck with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment of searching... and coming up empty. [pause] It sounds like something in you went quiet when that happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quieter] Yeah, it did. Like I've always got an answer for everything, right? Oh it's the job, oh it's just how we all blow off steam. But I sat there and I genuinely could not find... a single day. In I don't even know how long. And I just sat with that for a while and it was like... [pause] ...huh. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've always had the answer ready. And for the first time, you didn't. [pause] I'm curious — what do you think it means? Not what anyone else would say. What does it mean to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... [exhales slowly] ...I think I'm scared that it's bigger than I've been telling myself. Like I've been saying it's fine, it's fine, it's fine — and maybe I've been saying that because if I stop saying it then I have to actually look at it. And I don't — I don't know what I'd see.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of this together for a moment. You came back even though part of you was ready not to. You've carried this idea that drinking is just part of the job, part of who you are in that world. And then last week something cracked that open — you went looking for a sober day and couldn't find one, and instead of brushing past it, you sat with it. And right now, in this room, you're saying maybe the story you've been telling yourself is a way of not having to look too closely. [pause] That takes a real kind of honesty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [long pause] Yeah. I mean... yeah. I don't know what I want to do about any of it yet. But yeah. That's pretty much it.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining me today, Harold. I know doing this over video can feel a little different, but I want you to know we can go at whatever pace feels right for you. So... what's on your mind? What brought you to reach out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, uh... my doctor, she mentioned something at my last checkup. About my liver. Said the numbers were, uh, not great. And I saw something online about this kind of, you know, counseling. I don't know. I figured I'd see what it was about. It's probably not... I mean, I've just been having a drink or two in the evenings. To wind down. It's not like I'm out at bars or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something your doctor said gave you enough pause that you looked into this and actually showed up today. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. Yeah. I just... the evenings are long, you know? I retired about two years ago and I thought it'd be great. Golf, grandkids, all that. But my wife passed four years back, and my kids are busy, and... it's quiet. It's real quiet. The drinking kind of just crept up, if I'm being honest. I didn't really notice until the doctor said something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet crept up, and so did the drinking. What does that drink in the evening actually give you, Harold? When you pour it, what are you hoping for?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. It just... takes the edge off. Makes the house feel a little less... I don't know. Empty, I suppose. And then one becomes two, maybe three. And I just... I sit there watching the news and it's like... what am I even doing? I'm 65 years old and I don't know what I'm doing. My wife used to say I'd be lost without a schedule. She was right. I don't know that there's much point in changing at this stage, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're sitting in a quiet house that used to have someone in it, going through a routine that doesn't fit you anymore, and still asking yourself what's the point. And yet, part of you showed up here today. That part of you... I don't think it's ready to give up. I think it's still looking for something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, maybe. I do think about my grandkids. My daughter, she... she doesn't say anything but I can tell she worries. And I don't want to be a burden. I don't want them to be dealing with... you know. Some old man who drank himself into a problem. My wife would be... she'd be disappointed. She really would. I'm not the man I was when she was around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You lost your wife, then you lost your routine when you retired, and the drinking quietly filled that space — not because you wanted a problem, but because the evenings were unbearable without something to get through them. And now your doctor is concerned, you're concerned, and when you think about your daughter and your grandkids, there's a version of yourself you want to be for them — and you don't feel like that person right now. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's it exactly. I hadn't really, uh, laid it all out like that. Hearing it that way makes me feel like... maybe it makes sense that I ended up here. Like I didn't just fall apart — things happened. But I don't have to just keep going the way I've been going. I could maybe... I don't know. Try something different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You could try something different. What would that even look like for you, Harold? If things were a little better a few months from now — what would be different about your evenings?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'd like to... I used to do woodworking. Before everything. I had a whole setup in the garage and I just stopped. And maybe I'd call my daughter more. Not because I need something, just to talk. I think if I had something to do with my hands in the evenings, I wouldn't reach for the bottle as fast. I'm not saying I can fix everything. But... maybe I could start there.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — I'm gonna be straight with you, this is probably not how you wanted to spend your Thursday afternoon. [laughs softly] I'm Marcus. You don't have to pretend to be glad you're here, most people aren't. But I'm curious — just from your own perspective, what's your read on all this? What do you think is actually going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My read? My read is this is a complete — look, I'm here because some judge who's never met me in his life decided I need counseling. I don't need counseling. I need people to stay out of my business. I had two drinks. Two. And now I gotta sit here and do this... whatever this is. So that's my read.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two drinks and the whole system lands on you. Yeah. That's enraging.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. And I've done this before, you know. Sat in some office just like this, talked to some lady who kept nodding and scribbling stuff down, and at the end of it I had less money and less time and nothing was any different. So I don't... I don't really know what the point is supposed to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already done a round of this and it went nowhere — so walking in here with zero faith that today's any different? That makes total sense. I get it. I'm curious though... when you were doing it before, back then, was there anything you were hoping might actually change? Like, underneath all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. [pause] I don't know. My wife was still around then. She wanted me to get it together and I guess I thought maybe I would. [exhales] Didn't happen. So. [shrugs] Ancient history at this point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She mattered. Getting it together — for her, maybe for yourself too — that mattered. Even if it didn't end up working out the way you wanted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. [long pause] I mean I'm not gonna sit here and pretend drinking hasn't cost me things, because it has. The marriage. Almost my job now, apparently. My daughter... she's fifteen and she looks at me like I'm — [stops] Whatever. I just don't like being told what to do. By anyone. That's always been my thing. You back me into a corner, I shut down. Every time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just told me something really important. You can actually see it — the marriage, the job scare, your daughter. And you know yourself well enough to know that when someone forces your hand, the walls go up. Honestly? Most people don't get that far until like session five. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. [short, surprised laugh] Yeah, well. I've had a lot of time to think. [pause] I just... I don't want to keep losing things, you know? I'm thirty-eight. At some point it's like — how much more am I actually willing to give up before I do something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That question — how much more are you willing to give up — that didn't come from the judge. That's yours. So I want to ask you something, and take your time with it: what does it actually look like on the other side? If things were genuinely different a year from now, what does that life look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... like, having a real relationship with my kids that isn't just — it isn't just supervised visits and them acting weird around me. And showing up to work not worrying about whether someone's gonna smell something. [long pause] I hadn't really thought about it like that before. Like, what I actually want. Not what I'm supposed to say I want.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Last time we talked, things were already feeling pretty heavy. How's the week been since then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it is what it is, right? Sarah found the bottles in the garage and we had a whole thing. But I wasn't even - like, it wasn't that bad. Guys I served with, they had it way worse coming home. I had a few beers after a garbage week at work, that's all. She acts like I killed somebody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're holding up this comparison - what you went through over there, what your buddies went through - and against all that, a few beers feels pretty minor. And at the same time, things at home blew up again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, yeah. Nobody over there was worried about how many drinks you had - it was just, that was how you got through it. That's just... that's the culture, man. You come home and suddenly everyone's got opinions. My dad drank. His dad drank. Nobody made it into this whole... production. I don't know why she can't just - I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think Sarah is actually scared of when she finds those bottles?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. Losing me, I guess. Or maybe she already has and she just hasn't said it yet. Honestly? I think she's checked out. I think even if I stopped tomorrow she'd find something else to - ... I don't know why I even came in today. What's the point. Nothing's gonna change.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in anyway. After a week like that, feeling like maybe none of it matters - you still got in the car and drove here. I don't think people who've given up do that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My daughter asked me yesterday if I was gonna be at her birthday party. She's seven years old. Seven. She shouldn't be asking that. She should just - that should be a given, you know? And the way she looked at me when she asked... like she wasn't sure. I told her yeah, of course, and she just kind of nodded. Like she didn't fully believe me. That's... I keep thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just make sure I'm with you. The thing with Sarah - part of you has almost braced for it, like maybe it's already over. But your daughter asking you that question, that seven-year-old looking at you not quite sure if her dad will show up... that one didn't go away. That one's still sitting with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I don't want to be my father. I literally swore I wouldn't be him. And I'm standing in my garage hiding bottles like I'm sixteen years old and I'm thinking - when did this happen? Like I'm not - I'm not stupid, I know what it looks like. I just... I don't know how to stop. It's not like flipping a switch. It's not that easy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're right - it's not a switch. Nobody's asking you to flip one. But I'm curious: the version of you that shows up to that birthday party, the one she doesn't have to wonder about - what does life look like for that guy?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably... I don't know. He's more present, I guess. She's not looking at him like that. Maybe Sarah and I - I don't know if that ship's sailed, I honestly don't. But my daughter... she deserves a dad who's actually there. Not just physically there. Actually there. I'm not making any big promises, but... I think I want to figure out what trying actually looks like. For real this time.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Marcus. I'm glad you came in. So... how have things been since last week? I remember you were feeling like you'd turned a corner — I'm curious where things are sitting now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... okay, sort of. Not great. There was an incident at work again and my supervisor basically gave me an ultimatum, so. I'm not gonna pretend I'm here because I suddenly love therapy. But I've been — I don't know. I've been trying to do what we talked about. Some of it, anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been trying. Even when the week went sideways on you, even when showing up here wasn't your first choice — you're still here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I guess. I mean, I don't hate it here as much as I thought I would. The last therapist I saw, I always felt like he was just... waiting for me to admit I was the problem, you know? Like ticking boxes. This is different. I'll give you that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you saying that. ... You mentioned something happened at work again. What was going on for you when that hit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was just — the depression got bad last week, like really bad, and I... I drank more than I should have. Came in late a couple days. My supervisor pulled me in and I'm sitting there feeling like such a failure and I'm thinking, here we go again, same story, different year. I just — I don't know. It all kind of collapsed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "Here we go again." Like you've stood in that exact spot before and you're exhausted by it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. I'm so tired of it. And look, I know the drinking doesn't fix anything — I'm not an idiot. But when the depression gets that dark, it's like... it's the only thing that turns the volume down. Even for a couple hours. I don't know what else to do with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So when things get that heavy, the drinking is what you reach for because it actually does something — it gives you relief, at least for a little while. And at the same time, you're saying you can see what it's costing you. ... What does life look like for you, Marcus, when you imagine it going differently?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want... God. I want to not dread Mondays. I want to not feel like I'm one bad week away from losing my job, my apartment, everything. I have a daughter — she's eight. Amara. And I want her to see me as someone she can count on. Not... not this. Not whatever this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you, if that's okay. You came in today not entirely by choice. This week knocked you down — the depression, the drinking, work. And yet here you are, talking about Amara, and something in you just shifted when you said her name. You know what kind of father you want to be. That's not nothing, Marcus. That's actually everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, it is. I just — I don't know if I know how to get there. But I think I want to actually try. Not just because my boss said so. Like, for real this time.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this is a new place, new face — that's not nothing, especially if you've done this before. So... what's on your mind coming in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm here because I was basically told to be. I got discharged two days ago and the attending made it pretty clear this was the next step, so. Here I am. I don't really think it's going to be different than the last time or the time before that, but — yeah. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this before and it didn't stick. And now someone else is calling the shots again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And look — I'm not some addict, okay? I work twelve-hour shifts in an ER. Do you have any idea what that's like right now? I watched people die for two years straight during COVID. Like, alone, with no family, just... me holding a tablet up to a screen. So having a few glasses of wine when I get home is not — that's not a problem. That's just how I survive. That's how I don't completely lose my mind.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to carry. And I'm not going to sit here and tell you that's wrong — what you've been through is real, and it's heavy. What I'm hearing is that drinking has been the thing that actually works. The thing that gets you through the door and lets you sleep.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I don't know what else I'm supposed to do. I can't afford to fall apart — I have patients who need me. And I know how that sounds, like I'm using it as an excuse, and maybe I am, I don't know. It's just... nobody wants to hear how bad it actually got. They just want you to show up and do your job and not make it weird.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it look like when the drinking stops working?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. Last week I showed up to a shift and I wasn't — I wasn't drunk, but I wasn't sharp. And I gave someone the right medication but then I second-guessed myself for the entire rest of the shift. Like, did I actually check the chart? Did I? I hadn't told anyone that. I still haven't. I don't know why I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've never said that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. Because if I say it out loud it's... it's real. And I'm a good nurse. I have always been a good nurse, that is the one thing I knew about myself. And lately I've been watching myself turn into someone who — someone I would not want taking care of me, or anyone I loved. And that is... that's a terrifying thing to notice about yourself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm tracking. You came in today because you felt like you had no choice — not because you wanted to be here. And the drinking has made sense, given what you've lived through. You're not ready to throw a label on it or sign up for anything. But somewhere underneath all of that there's this nurse — the one you've always been — and she is scared. Scared about what she might miss. About who she's becoming. That part of you showed up today too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I didn't come in here planning to say any of that. I'm still not — I don't know what I'm ready for. But yeah. I'm worried. I think I've been worried for a while and just kept... kept burying it under the next shift.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in today. I know walk-in appointments can feel a little... I don't know, unexpected sometimes. I just want you to know there's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through. I'm just curious — what's on your mind today, what brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My girlfriend basically made me come. Like, she — yeah. She gave me this whole ultimatum thing and I figured whatever, I'd come in, see what this is. I don't really think I have a problem or anything, I just... she's been on my case lately and it was easier to just show up than keep fighting about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So she matters enough to you that you came, even if you're not totally sure this is the right place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Yeah, she does. She said — she actually said she'd leave. Like, those words. And that kind of freaked me out, I'm not gonna lie. But the thing is, what she's upset about is just... it's normal stuff. I go out on weekends, I drink with my friends. Every single person I know does the same thing. I'm a senior in college, that's just — that's what you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is scared about losing her... and at the same time, another part of you is looking around at your life and thinking, I don't see a problem here. Those two things are sitting in the same place right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Like — okay, sure, sometimes I drink a lot. But it's not like I'm some alcoholic sitting alone with a bottle, you know? It's social. It's with people. My boys, we pregame, we go out, whatever. Last weekend everyone got just as wrecked as me and nobody's girlfriend is dragging them to counseling. So... I don't know. It feels like I'm being singled out and I don't really get why.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not trying to avoid this conversation — you walked in here, and that says something. I'm also hearing that there's a piece of you that actually wants to understand what she's seeing, even if right now it doesn't fully add up for you. What do you think it is that she's worried about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I don't know, she says I change when I drink. Like I get loud, I say stuff. There was this one time — I don't even remember it that well — but she said I was, like, really mean to her at this party and I just... I don't remember it the way she does. And she keeps bringing that up. But that was one time. People say things when they're drunk, that's not — that doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there are these moments you can't fully account for... and she's been holding onto one of them. I'm wondering — when you try to imagine what it's like to be on her side of that, watching someone you love and not recognizing them... what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... that would suck. That would genuinely suck. I don't want to be that guy, like I'm not trying to be a bad boyfriend. And I do care about her, I really do. I just — I'm not ready to say that drinking is the whole problem. That feels like a big leap. But maybe... I don't know, maybe there's something to look at there. I'm not saying she's wrong about everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in not sure what to expect, feeling a little pushed into this... and somewhere in the middle of this conversation, something shifted just a little. You're not ready to name it all, and that's okay. There's no rush. What would it mean to you — just for you, separate from her — to get a little clearer on this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly... I think it would just feel better. Like, not having this thing hanging over everything. She and I have been together two years, and I don't want it to blow up over something I could've — I don't know. I'm not making any promises or whatever. But maybe I could come back. Talk more. See what comes up.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you made it in today. I know the waiting room out there isn't exactly comfortable. Um, there's no real agenda I'm trying to push on you — we can just talk. So in your own words, what's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... my supervisor — I still pick up shifts at the hardware store, keeps me busy you know — he said I had to come in after... after the thing that happened last month. So. I'm not really sure what I'm supposed to say here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here because someone else thought it was a good idea, and you're not quite sure what this is all about. That makes a lot of sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Pretty much. I mean — look, I'm not gonna pretend like everything's been perfect. Since I retired, it's... it's been quieter than I expected. My wife passed a couple years back and the kids are — they've got their own lives. Which is fine. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like things got very quiet, very fast — and you've been carrying a lot of that on your own. What's the drinking been like for you in the middle of all that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah, I have a few drinks in the evening. More than I used to, I'll admit that. My doctor mentioned something at my last checkup — liver numbers or whatever — and I told him it wasn't a big deal. But then at work I... I don't even really remember what happened exactly. I just — I wasn't myself and it scared me a little, if I'm being honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It scared you. Something happened that felt out of character — not like the man you know yourself to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, it did. I spent thirty-some years in the Army and I was always — I was the reliable one. That was my thing. And now I'm sitting in a house by myself at six in the afternoon pouring another glass and I think... what would my wife say. What would she think of me right now. She'd be worried sick.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That reliability — being the one people could count on — that's clearly something that means a great deal to you. And it sounds like part of you is noticing a real gap between who you've always been and where things have been heading. What would it look like for you to start feeling like yourself again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... getting out of the house more, I guess. Having something to do. When I was working full-time there was structure, there was — there was a reason to get up. Now it's just... days. And the drinking fills the time. But it's not making me feel better. I know that. I've known that for a while, if I'm honest with myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm hearing you right. Since retirement things got quiet in a way you weren't prepared for — and especially after losing your wife. The drinking kind of crept in to fill that space, but you've been aware for some time now that it isn't really helping. And then what happened at work shook something loose. The man you've always been — steady, dependable, someone people rely on — you want to find your way back to him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...That's about right. Yeah. I think I've just been waiting for someone to say it like that. I don't want to end up like this. I really don't. I just — I don't quite know where to start.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... you said it was a hard week. I want to hear about it — all of it, whatever feels right to start with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had a group show. Small gallery, people I actually respect, and my friend Maya — she's not even an artist, she's a graphic designer, which, fine — she pulls me aside and tells me my new pieces feel 'distant.' Like emotionally flat. And I've been... okay so I've been drinking more lately, trying to get back into it, trying to find that thing again, and everyone acts like that's the problem but they don't — they don't understand how it works for me. It loosens something. It always has. Maya doesn't know what she's talking about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Someone you trust looked at your work — work you'd put real effort into — and said it was missing something. And that landed hard. Like a verdict, almost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. I mean I'm not — I'm not some... I'm not falling apart, I function, I show up, I make things. Or I did. This week I sat in front of a canvas for like four hours and just... nothing. Poured myself a glass to get out of my head and it didn't do anything. So I had another and then it was midnight and I hadn't touched a brush. That's not — that's not how it's supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The thing that was supposed to unlock the door... isn't opening it anymore. And that's frightening, because for you the art isn't just a job — it's proof that you're still you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...exactly. God. It used to be, like, one glass and things would just — loosen. Colors looked different. I'd stop second-guessing every mark. Now I'm having way more than that and there's just... nothing there. Static. And I keep telling myself it's a block, or stress, or the pressure of the show. But honestly I don't know anymore if the drinking is opening me up or just... turning the volume down on everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does your gut say — when you really sit with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I think I've been telling myself this story. For years. That alcohol is the muse, it's the fuel, it's how I access the real stuff. And maybe — I mean this is terrifying to say out loud — maybe I built that story because I was scared. Scared that if I took it away I'd find out there was nothing underneath. That the creativity was always just... the alcohol. Not me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Saying that out loud takes guts. A lot of people hold onto the story their whole lives rather than look at what's underneath it. You just looked.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I keep thinking about my early work. Like, mid-twenties, before all this really set in. And I was making things that — I don't know, they felt alive. And I want that back. Not the career stuff, not the shows, just... that feeling that something real came out of me. I actually want that back. I didn't realize how much until right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think something important happened today. You came in angry — at Maya, at the show, maybe at yourself a little. And underneath that anger was something much harder: the fear that the thing you've depended on for years might actually be working against you now. You've held onto the belief that alcohol unlocks your creativity, and that belief made sense for a long time. But you're noticing the art has changed. The hours at the canvas aren't producing anything. And you just said something you've maybe never said before — that you're afraid there's nothing underneath. And also that you want to find out if there is. That's not the same person who walked in here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it's not. I don't know what trying something different looks like yet, but... I think I'm ready to actually find out. For the first time in a long time I think I actually want to know.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, grab a seat wherever you're comfortable. I appreciate you coming in today. I know walking into a new place like this isn't always easy. So — what brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife. She gave me an ultimatum — basically said if I don't come talk to somebody she's done. So. Here I am. But I'll be upfront with you, I've done the counseling thing before, couple different guys, and it was a complete waste of my time. So I don't really know what you think is gonna be different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been through this before, it went nowhere, and now you're back in a chair because the stakes feel higher than they've ever been. That's a tough spot to be in — and I don't blame you for being skeptical.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Skeptical's a nice word for it. Look, I don't — I don't think I have some big drinking problem. Okay? Guys drink. We always drank. You spend fourteen months in a combat zone and then come back and tell me what you do to turn your brain off at night. It's... I mean it's just what you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking was part of how you and the guys managed everything you were carrying over there. It worked. It still works, in some ways.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. It's not like I'm some — I'm not sitting in a gutter somewhere, alright? I have a job, I show up, I pay the bills. But apparently none of that matters. Apparently I'm the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say none of it matters to anyone — tell me more about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's... my wife's not wrong that I'm different when I drink. I get... I get short with people. Short-tempered. And my son — he's seven — he, um... he gets scared of me sometimes. And that's... I mean, that's not okay. I know that's not okay. I just don't know how you fix something like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's the part that really gets to you. Your son being scared of you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah. I didn't — I didn't go through two deployments to come home and be that guy. I don't want to be my dad. He was a... he wasn't around, let's put it that way. And I swore I wouldn't — I just, I don't know what I'm supposed to do. But I can't keep being that for him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you. You came in here skeptical — which, honestly, makes complete sense given what you've been through. And in the same breath, you told me you've held down a job, you've kept your family together, you survived two deployments. And then something shifted when you talked about your son. That matters. That's not a small thing — that's you knowing exactly what you're fighting for. That's a real place to start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I'm not promising anything. I want to be clear about that. But I'm here, right? I actually walked in, so... I don't know. Maybe that's something.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Before we get into anything... I just want to say, you're here. That matters. I know this kind of appointment isn't always something people choose for themselves. So — what brings you in today, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Honestly? My sister basically guilted me into coming. She's been on my case about... stuff. I've had a rough couple years, which — I mean, who hasn't, right? But I'm managing. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's worried about you. And part of you maybe isn't so sure she's completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... she's not totally wrong. I've been drinking more than I probably should, but — okay, I work twelve-hour shifts in an ER. Do you know what that's like? You see things. And at the end of it I just need to turn my brain off somehow. It's not like I'm some... like, it's not a problem problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about one of those shifts. What does a night actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... okay. Last week we had a fourteen-year-old come in. Car accident. And there was just — there was nothing we could do. And then I had to walk back out there, you know? Clock still running. You compartmentalize. You have to. And then I drove home at like 2am and I poured a glass and then another and I didn't even feel bad about it until the morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You hold all of that... inside your chest. And then you drive home alone with it at 2am. That sounds like an incredibly heavy thing to carry, over and over.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It is. And — I don't know. I've been making some mistakes at work lately. Nothing catastrophic, but I forgot to chart a medication update last month and my supervisor pulled me aside. And I know why. I know it's because I'm running on empty. I just — I'm not ready to say out loud that it's the drinking doing that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty. You didn't have to go there, and you did. That tells me something about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm just... tired. Tired of pretending I'm okay. The drinking started as like, a survival thing — during COVID we were just, it was insane in there, and it helped me sleep. And now it's just... I don't know if I can do the job without it, and I don't know if I can keep doing the job with it. That's kind of a horrible place to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're caught — between a job that clearly means everything to you, and something that started as survival and is now getting in the way of you being the nurse you actually want to be. And underneath all of it, I'm hearing someone who hasn't given up. What would it mean for you if things started to feel different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I think I'd feel like myself again. I used to actually love this job. Like, I chose it. I miss that person. Maybe — I don't know where to start, but maybe that's what I'm here for.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in. I know you didn't have a lot of choice in that, so... that's not lost on me. I also know you've sat in rooms like this one before and it didn't go anywhere. I'm not going to pretend I have something they didn't. What I'd like to do is just — hear from you. What's going on for you right now, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... look. I'm here because the advisor said I had to be here or there'd be consequences. So. Here I am. I've done three of these — three different counselors — and it's the same every time. 'Tell me about your drinking, Marcus. How does that make you feel.' And nothing changes. I don't know what you think is gonna be different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three counselors. Three times sitting in a chair being asked to explain yourself. And here you are doing it again — because someone else decided you should be. That's exhausting. And honestly, a little demeaning.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. And you know what the kicker is? I'm not even — look, I drink. Okay? I drink. But I served two tours. Fallujah, then Kandahar. I came back and I couldn't sleep, couldn't — I don't know, function, without a few drinks. Half my unit drinks way more than me. Nobody's sending them to a counselor. Nobody's making them sit here and justify themselves.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What you came back carrying — I'm not going to pretend I understand that. I don't. And drinking being part of military culture, being how guys held it together over there and after... that's real. That's not something I'm here to argue with. ... What I keep coming back to, though, is — you walked through that door. Something got you here beyond just following orders.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife. She — look, she doesn't get it either. She thinks I have a problem. Everyone thinks Marcus has a problem. Nobody ever stops to ask what Marcus had to do to get through two deployments, what he saw, what he — nobody asks that. They just see a guy with a beer in his hand and they've got him all figured out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She said something that scared you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said she's... she said she's done. That she'll take the kids to her mom's if I don't — I don't know — 'get help' or whatever. Which is — I mean I'm not gonna just stop being who I am because she's — ugh. It's not that simple. It's not like I can just flip a switch. I don't even know if I... I mean, it's complicated. It's just real complicated.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not willing to just... disappear yourself because someone's telling you to. I hear that. That's not weakness, that's someone who knows who he is. ... But your kids. When you think about them not being there when you get home — what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My son's seven. He does this thing — when I come home he runs and jumps and I catch him and he just — he trusts me completely, you know? Like I'm the safest thing in the world. And I... I don't want to lose that. I don't want to be my dad. My dad was never there. I swore I'd never be that. I'm not saying I have a drinking problem. I'm saying I don't want to lose my kids.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying so much for so long — two deployments, coming home to a world that didn't know how to receive you, a wife who's at her limit, a system that keeps sending you to rooms like this one. And underneath all of it... there's a father who is terrified of becoming someone his son doesn't get to have. That part — I don't want to rush past that. That's not nothing. That's everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess that's — yeah. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with any of this. I'm not making any promises. But I'm... I'm here. For now.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Go ahead and take a seat wherever you're comfortable. I'm Dr. Chen. No agenda for the first few minutes — just... whatever brought you in today, we can start there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well — [shifts in seat, arms crossed] I didn't exactly choose to be here, so. The court's making me do this. You probably already got that in whatever file they sent you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's that like — being told you have to show up somewhere?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you think it's like? [exhales hard] I'm a thirty-eight year old man. I've got a job, I've got my kids every other week — I don't need some judge telling me I gotta sit in a room and talk about my feelings. I had a couple drinks, made a bad call. Now the whole system comes down on me like I'm... I don't know. Like I'm some kind of criminal or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's real anger there — feeling like this is way out of proportion to what happened. And it sounds like part of what stings is how it looks. Like it doesn't match who you actually are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Because it doesn't. [leans forward] This is my second time, okay, I know how that sounds. But I'm not some — I don't fit whatever picture they've got in their head. My dad was a drinker. Like, a real drinker. I know what that looks like, and that's not me. I can stop whenever I want. I just... I don't always want to, I guess. [catches himself] That came out wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, I think that came out pretty honest, actually. [pause] You mentioned your dad. And you said you know what that looks like. That's not nothing — carrying that awareness all these years. [pause] I'm curious about something though. You said this is the second time. What do you make of that yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... [long pause, looks at hands] I don't know. I know how it looks. Two DUIs, same guy — I'm not an idiot, I can do the math on that. My buddy Marcus, he's the one who actually pushed me to come here. He said... [quieter] he said, 'You're one more night away from losing everything.' And I just — I couldn't really argue with him. I wanted to, but. [shrugs] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Marcus put into words something you'd maybe already been sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think so. [voice quieter now] Look, I don't — my kids, that's not something I'm willing to mess with. That's the line for me. And lately I keep thinking... what am I doing? Like, what am I actually doing? I swore I'd never be my dad. I swore that. [pause, jaw tightens briefly, then loosens] I don't want to be that guy that they're scared of. Or embarrassed by. My daughter's twelve. She's paying attention.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, see if I've got it right. You came in here today feeling forced — and that frustration is completely legitimate. And at the same time, there's another part of you that already knew something before you walked through that door. Marcus' words landed because they were true. Your daughter's watching. You made a promise to yourself a long time ago about who you weren't going to be. And now you're here, kind of... taking stock of all that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [sits back, uncrosses arms for the first time] Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. [quiet for a moment] I still think the whole DUI enforcement thing is... whatever, that's a different conversation. But my part in it. [exhales slowly] Maybe I can look at my part. I'm not saying I'm an alcoholic or whatever label you want to put on it. But I'm... I'm willing to talk. I think.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in today. I know this isn't easy — new place, someone you've never met, no reason yet to trust any of it. There's no checklist I need to get through. No form I'm filling out in my head. I just... want to understand what's going on for you, if you're willing to share that.

utterances.speaker: client
