utterances.text: Look, I'll be straight with you. I've done this. Sat in these rooms, talked to — no offense — guys like you. And nothing changed. My wife basically told me show up or she's done, so. [gestures around] Here I am. Don't take it personal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That actually takes something — showing up when you don't believe it's going to help. ... What's it been like, the other times you've tried this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Same thing every time. They wanna tell me I got a problem. Like — okay, yeah, I drink. I was in Fallujah. Two tours. You drink over there, man, everyone drinks, it's just — it's how you get through it. Coming home doesn't mean you just... flip a switch. That's not how it works. And I don't think that's something any counselor's gonna be able to explain away for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found something over there that helped you survive. And drinking was part of that. ... And now people are asking you to put it down like it's simple — like they have any idea what you were carrying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. [pause] And look, I've tried. Cut back before — like three weeks, almost a month. Then something happens and I'm right back. So I don't... I don't know what the point is anymore. I think this is just — this is just who I am now. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three weeks. That wasn't nothing, Ryan. Something in you wanted things to be different — enough to actually try. ... [long silence] You mentioned your wife brought you here. What does she see that has her this scared?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She says I'm not... present. Like even when I'm in the room, I'm not there. And the kids — my son's seven, my daughter just turned four — they'll come up to me and I'm just... [exhales, looks at floor] She told me last month — she said, Ryan, they're scared of you sometimes. And I didn't even — [voice tightens] — I didn't know that. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ... What was it like to hear that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Worst thing I've ever heard. Worse than — [stops] — worse than anything over there. [long pause] I don't want to be that guy. I love my kids. I love Sarah. That's not... that's not the dad I wanted to be. That's not — I don't know, maybe it's too late, but that's not what I want.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I've got this right, because I don't want to miss anything. You came in today not expecting much — you've been here before, and it hasn't stuck, and part of you wonders if it ever will. And you've been carrying something enormous since you came back — something most people will never understand. And then last month, your wife said something that hit different than any of it. Your kids are scared. And that — that landed somewhere nothing else has. Because being their dad, being present for them — that's not something you're willing to lose.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quietly] Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's right. [pause] I don't know how to do this. I genuinely don't. But I don't want my son remembering his dad like that. I don't want that. So I guess I'm — I don't know — willing to try again. For real this time. Maybe.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for logging on today — I know this isn't always the easiest thing to do, especially when it wasn't entirely your idea. Your sister mentioned she's been worried about you. I'm curious, what was it like for you, making the decision to come today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly, I almost didn't. My sister means well, she just... she doesn't get it. She doesn't have kids, she doesn't know what I deal with every single day. I'm not — I want to be clear, I'm not some kind of alcoholic. I drink wine at the end of the day to decompress. That's all it is. I just figured if I came, at least she'd get off my back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the end of the day — that's the one time that's yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. I get them to bed, and it's like... finally. I pour a glass and I sit and I don't have to be anyone's mom for like an hour. I'm not hurting anyone. It's just... I mean, one glass has sort of turned into — you know. It's more than one glass now. But I'm functioning. I show up. I do everything I'm supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that look like — a typical night, once the kids are down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I open the bottle and I tell myself one glass. And then I just... keep going until it's gone. And then I wake up exhausted and I feel awful about myself, and then I just do it all over again that night. I don't even think it relaxes me anymore, honestly. I think I'm past that. I don't know how to stop. Like I genuinely don't know who I am at 9 PM without it. That's... that probably sounds bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound bad. It sounds like someone who has been carrying an enormous amount completely alone, for a very long time — and found the one thing that gave her a moment of relief. And now even that thing doesn't feel like relief anymore. Just... a hole you fall into every night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — yeah. That's exactly it. And I keep thinking about my daughter. She's twelve, she's not oblivious. She sees the recycling. She's seen me some mornings. I just... I don't want to be that mom. I'm so scared of being that mom. My mom was — never mind. I just don't want to do that to them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it's worth naming clearly. You showed up today even though part of you didn't want to. You described a cycle that's stopped giving you what you need, and you've been watching yourself in it — aware of it. And underneath all of that, there's this very specific thing you're protecting: your kids. Your relationship with them. The kind of mom you want to be. That's not a small thing. That's actually a really powerful reason.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never really... thought about it like that. I just feel like I've been failing for so long that it stopped feeling like failing — it just felt like life. But I don't want to fail them. That's the one thing I know. And if there's some way to get through the evenings without feeling like I'm crawling out of my skin... I'd want to try that. I think I would.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said you'd want to try. I don't want to gloss over that — that matters. That's not where you were ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, it's not. I think I've just been telling myself it's fine for so long that I forgot to check if it actually was. I don't know what any of this looks like going forward, I'm not going to pretend I have it figured out. But I'm here. And I came back after the first five minutes, which, honestly — that's more than I expected from myself today.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to start by acknowledging that you came back. That wasn't a given, and it means something. Last week felt a little rough toward the end, so I'm curious — what was it like for you after you left?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I almost didn't come. Sat in the parking lot for like fifteen minutes. My wife basically... look, she made it pretty clear I didn't have a choice. But I'm not gonna sit here and pretend I think this is necessary, because I don't. I've been drinking the same way since I got back and I've been fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because of pressure from her, and another part of you is sitting with this feeling that nothing is actually wrong on your end.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Look, where I served, everybody drank. After a patrol, after a bad week — that's just what you did. Nobody called it a problem. It was how you dealt. And now I'm home and suddenly it's a problem because my wife read something online or whatever. The guys I deployed with, half of them drink way more than me. That's just... that's the culture, man. I'm not some — I'm not an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sense of belonging — drinking as something that connected you to the guys you served with, that made hard things survivable. That clearly still matters to you. I want to ask you something, and you don't have to answer any particular way. When you picture how things look six months from now... if nothing changes... what do you see?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. She'll probably leave. She said she would. I keep thinking she's bluffing but... I don't know anymore. She's not — she's not someone who bluffs. And I just. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with that. Because even if I — even if I cut back or whatever, what does that fix? The damage is already done, right? It's probably already too late.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot of pain underneath that. Like you're already grieving something you haven't fully lost yet, and part of you has almost... accepted that it's gone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's kind of it. I love her. I do. And my kids — my son is seven and he asked me last week why mom was crying and I didn't have an answer for him. That's... that's not okay. I know that's not okay. I'm not — I'm not blind to it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just did something important. You named it — your son asking why mom was crying, and you sitting there without an answer. That took something to say out loud. That's a man who still cares deeply about his family. What does being a good father mean to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means... not being my dad. My dad was checked out. He wasn't violent or anything, just — gone. Even when he was in the room. And I swore I wasn't gonna be that. And now I'm sitting here and I'm like... am I that? Is that what I've become? Because I don't — I don't want that for him. I don't want him to look back and think I was just... absent.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, because I think there's more here than you maybe walked in with today. You came back — you sat in the parking lot and you came in anyway. You're someone who was shaped by a culture where drinking was survival, where it meant brotherhood. And at the same time, there's a part of you that's watching your son, thinking about your father, and knowing that the man you want to be is still reachable. Those two things are both true, and that tension — that's not weakness. That's actually where change starts.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... I never really thought about it like that. Like, I've been thinking of this as her problem with me. But when you say it that way... I don't know, man. Maybe there's something worth — I'm not saying I'm ready to do anything drastic. But maybe it's worth at least figuring out what this would even look like. For my kids, if nothing else.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for getting on today, Gerald. I know telehealth can feel a little odd — how's your connection, can you hear me okay? Good. So before we get into anything formal, I just want to start simply: tell me, in your own words, what's been going on lately.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor sent me here. Said I needed to talk to someone. I mean — look, I know what this is. I've done AA, I've done the programs, I know the whole deal. I relapsed, okay? I know I did. But she basically said she'd be worried if I didn't show up, so... that's why I'm here. Not because I think this is gonna fix anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because you felt pushed into it. Not really your choice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, yeah. I mean — look, I lost my job. Twenty-two years at the same company. Same desk, same people. And then one day it's layoffs, here's your severance, don't let the door hit you on the way out. And two months later I'm drinking again and suddenly everybody's very concerned about Gerald. Where was all that concern when I got handed a cardboard box, huh?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years and then just — gone. That's not just a job, that's a real loss. And you stayed sober through a lot in those three years before this. I'm curious... what was that time like for you? Being sober that long?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was — it was good. It was real. I had my routines, I had my sponsor, I was showing up to meetings. My kids were starting to trust me again, you know? My daughter actually — she let me come to her daughter's birthday. My granddaughter. First time they'd let me come to something like that in... years. And now I've just thrown all of that away. So yeah. It was great. And now it's over.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those three years weren't just about not drinking. They meant something. Your granddaughter's birthday. Your kids letting you back in. You're carrying this weight right now that all of that is somehow erased — that one relapse wipes out everything you built.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Doesn't it though? I mean... three years and I couldn't hold it together the second something went wrong. What does that say about me? I just — I don't know. Maybe this is just... who I am. Maybe that's all there is to it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say maybe this is just who you are — I want to stay there for a second, because you also just described someone who built three years of sobriety from the ground up. Who showed up to meetings. Who repaired things with his kids well enough to be at his granddaughter's birthday. Who is that person to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I don't know. He's still in there somewhere, I guess. I think about my son — he called me last week. First time in a while. And he doesn't know I've been drinking again, and I just... I didn't tell him. I didn't want to. Because I don't want to be that guy again. Not for him. Not for any of them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, because I think there's a lot here. You came in today feeling pushed — like the system flagged a relapse but nobody noticed a layoff that took twenty-two years of your life in one afternoon. And underneath that anger, there's someone who knows exactly what sobriety felt like. What it cost him to get there, and what it gave back — his kids, his granddaughter, his son calling. And even right now, in the middle of this, part of you is protecting something. You didn't tell your son because you don't want to be that person again. That part of you hasn't gone anywhere, Gerald.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it hasn't. I just... I got lost for a minute. Longer than a minute, maybe. But no — I don't want to stay in this place. I've come back before, I know I have. I just gotta figure out how to do it when everything falls apart all at once. Because I didn't have a plan for that. I just... didn't.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it can take a lot to walk through that door for the first time — really. I'd love to just start by hearing from you, in your own words, what brought you in to see me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... yeah. So my advisor kind of mentioned it. She wasn't like, forcing me or anything, she just — she noticed I'd been off lately. And I've been thinking about it for a while and... I drink a lot. Like, at social things. Every social thing, really. And I know it's a lot, I just — I don't know. I feel kind of stupid saying it out loud for the first time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like alcohol has become something you really rely on when you're around other people. And there's something painful about recognizing that — even saying it out loud feels hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I've tried, like — I've told myself a hundred times, 'just two drinks, that's it.' And then it's never two drinks. And the next morning I just feel... worse. About everything. I think this might just be who I am. Like maybe I'm just someone who needs it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've tried to change this on your own, more than once, and it hasn't gone the way you hoped — and that's been really discouraging. What I also notice is that you keep trying. That tells me something important about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. It doesn't feel like trying. It feels like failing over and over. Without alcohol I'm just... I'm the person standing in the corner of the room wanting to disappear. I genuinely do not know who I am at a party sober. That's a scary thing to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to stay with something you just said — 'I don't know who I am sober in those moments.' If you could somehow have that ease, that ability to connect with people, without needing alcohol to get there... what would that version of your life look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. I haven't really thought about it that way. I guess... I'd actually remember conversations? Like I have these friends and I sometimes wonder if they know me, or if they just know drunk me. And I don't totally know the difference anymore either. That's kind of a weird thing to realize right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing. You came in because someone you trust nudged you, but part of you was already aware something felt off. You've tried to pull back on your own and it hasn't worked, and that's left you feeling stuck and kind of hopeless about it. And now you're sitting with this new question — whether the people close to you actually know the real you, and whether you know her. Does that feel like I'm tracking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's all of it. I haven't said any of that out loud before, ever. It's a lot to hear back. But also kind of... I don't know, like a relief? Like at least someone else knows it now. It's not just rattling around in my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to say all of that for the very first time. The fact that you walked in here today, that you're willing to look at this honestly — that's not nothing. That's actually a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thank you. I... yeah. I think I want to figure this out. Like, I don't want to be 35 and still needing three glasses of wine just to make eye contact with someone. That's not — that's not the life I want. I think I actually want to try.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned you had about twenty minutes before your next class, so I want to make sure we use your time well. What's going on that made you reach out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know, I just... okay, so I've been drinking more than I probably should. Like a bottle of wine most nights. But I'm a single mom, I have two kids, my ex is basically useless, and I work full time, so — I mean, it's not like I'm drinking in the morning or anything. I just need something to wind down. I think I just maybe wanted to, like, check in. Make sure I'm not, you know... going off the rails.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand, you've got a really full plate — single parenting, work, doing it mostly alone — and the wine helps you come down from all of that. And on the other hand, something made you show up here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. It's like — okay, I know a bottle a night is a lot. I'm not stupid. But what am I supposed to do? I get home at seven, the kids need dinner, there's homework, there's always something broken or someone crying, and by nine I'm just... I'm done. I need something that's just mine, you know? Something that actually works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said something made you want to come in — a wake-up call. What happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter — she's twelve — she came downstairs last Thursday and I was on my second glass and she just... she looked at me. She didn't say anything, she just had this face. Like she was checking on me. And she's twelve! She shouldn't be checking on me, I'm supposed to be checking on her. And I just — God, I got so angry, not at her, just at the whole situation, and I put the glass down and I couldn't sleep all night. I just kept thinking, like, when did this become my thing? When did this become what I do?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — your daughter's face — it cut through something. You're carrying an enormous amount, and the wine has been the one thing that makes the weight feel bearable. But that moment showed you a cost you hadn't quite let yourself see before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I keep telling myself it's fine because I'm functional, right? Like I show up, I do everything I'm supposed to do. But she looked at me the way I used to look at my mom when I was a kid, and my mom had a real problem, and I just... I don't want to be that. I don't want her to grow up and be sitting somewhere talking about me the way I'd talk about my mom.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You recognized that look because you lived it — and the fact that it stopped you cold, that you couldn't sleep, that you're sitting here right now? That's not someone going off the rails. That's someone who still has their compass.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I haven't thought about it that way. I've just been kind of beating myself up, like I should've caught this sooner. But maybe — I don't know. Maybe the fact that it bothered me that much means something. Like, I do actually want to change it. I just have no idea what I'd do instead. The wine is easy. It's reliable. But... yeah. I think I want to figure something else out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you've covered a lot of ground in twenty minutes. You're under real, relentless pressure — and the wine became your pressure valve. It works, in the short term. But your daughter's face showed you a version of the future you don't want, and you're somebody who pays attention to that. You're not asking whether to change — you're already past that. You're asking how. That's a very different starting place than most people come in with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think that's right. I have to go in a minute but... can I come back? Like, I think I actually want to work on this. I don't know what that looks like yet but — I showed up today, so. That's something, right?

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey. So... I know this probably wasn't your idea, coming in today. And I just want to say upfront — I'm not here to lecture you, and I'm not reporting anything back to your parents. That's not how this works. I'm just... curious about you, honestly. What's it like for you, being here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. I don't really want to be here. No offense. My parents are just — they freaked out over nothing and now I'm sitting here so. Whatever. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting, this whole thing feels like a lot of reaction to something that isn't actually a big problem.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like every kid drinks. I'm not... I don't have some problem. I had a few bottles in my room, big deal. My parents act like they found, I don't know, a body or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. I'm wondering — and you don't have to answer this if you don't want to — but when your mom or your dad actually found those bottles... what was going through your head in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... nothing. I don't know. I was just — I'd hidden them pretty good, so I didn't think they'd find them. And then my mom's just standing there holding them and she's got this look on her face and I just... look, can we talk about something else? It's fine. It's over.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That look on her face is still sitting with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. I mean. She wasn't even yelling. She was just — scared. Like genuinely scared. And that's somehow worse, you know? She's been through a lot, my mom. And I didn't think it was gonna be like that. I thought she'd just be mad and ground me or whatever and that'd be it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you actually care a lot about her. And you didn't want to be the reason she felt scared. I'm curious — what do you think you were looking for, when you started keeping those bottles around? Like what was going on for you at the time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's gonna sound stupid. Things at home have just been... a lot. And then at work too, my supervisor's always on my case, and then the thing happened and — I don't know. When I'd drink it just kind of made everything go quiet for a little while.
